content_blocks.html: Want to know your voice will come through before the meeting starts? This mic test is a quick microphone test that shows your waveform, plays your audio back and stays private, with no install and no uploads. It works on all devices, so you can speak, watch the meter move and check how your listeners will receive you.

Online Mic Test: Real-Time Waveform and Volume Meter

This mic test online uses a free microphone tool that listens through your browser and draws a real-time sound wave as you speak. A moving volume meter and a visual wave show your input level and peak at a glance, so you can judge loudness without guessing. Clear audio clarity shows up as a wave that rises and falls with your words; a flat line means nothing is arriving. For a different check, see the full list of free online microphone and speaker tests.

Pick the Right Input Device

Use the input device selector to find and select microphone hardware when you own several microphones. Your default input is not always the right pick, so confirm it here and speak into it for a moment before trusting the sound.

Microphone Information: Sample Rate and Latency

The tester also lists a quality rating and what your browser opened: sample rate, sample size, audio channels, latency, echo cancellation, noise suppression and auto gain. Those flags tell you whether the system is quietly altering your voice, while the gain setting decides how loud you arrive.

What This Microphone Test Checks

It checks that permission is granted, that signal is present, and how hot you run. What you can see, you can fix.

How to Test Your Microphone in Four Steps

You can test your microphone online in under a minute. No downloads and no signups are needed on this website, so it is an easy way for studio newcomers and veterans alike to test my mic or use a microphone checker before a session.

  1. Press Start on the page.
  2. Allow microphone permissions when asked.
  3. Speak naturally and watch the meter and waveform.
  4. Stop, then listen back so you can listen to yourself.

Allow Microphone Access in Your Browser

Choose Allow on the prompt. Without access to your microphone, no signal reaches the page, and the browser microphone permission can stay blocked until you reopen the lock icon beside the address bar.

Input Level and Background Noise Check

Talk at a normal level for five seconds, then stay silent for three. Your input level should jump while you talk and sink during the pause; a meter that stays busy in silence reveals background noise from fans or other sounds in the room.

Mic Check With Playback, Loopback and Recording

A fast check is useful, but a test with playback tells you more. Record a short clip and listen to playback quality, then try a mic loopback test to hear yourself live and notice any delay. Add a mic volume test by speaking at your quietest and loudest. Together they suit a podcast take or any take, and each step is a short loop.

Wear Headphones to Avoid Echo and Feedback

Loopback sends your signal straight to your speakers, which can cause feedback. Put on headphones so the mic cannot pick up its own output, and keep the diaphragm of desk microphones away from the speaker.

Download an MP3 or WAV Recording

The page uses the browser's MediaRecorder to capture a clip, and you can download it as MP3 for a small file or WAV for uncompressed audio. The download stays on your computer.

Test the Mic Online Before a Podcast Interview: A Worked Example

Priya has a podcast interview at 4 p.m. and a new USB mic she has never recorded with. The decision: keep the dial where the box left it, or turn it down? She opens the microphone tester, picks the USB device from the selector, leaves the browser's level boost off and counts to five out loud to judge the sound quality.

The tester's meter reads a peak of 0.71 of full scale, which is -3.0 dB, and during three seconds of silence the silent-room reading is 0.0021, or -53.6 dB; a hand check with 20 × log₁₀(0.71) agrees. Against the common target of speech peaks between -12 and -6 dB, that is hot: one laugh from her guest would hit the 0 dB ceiling and clip.

So she cuts the gain by 6 dB, which halves the amplitude (a 6.02 dB drop for a factor of two), and checks again:

Gain settingPeakNoise floorGap
As shipped0.71 (-3.0 dB)0.0021 (-53.6 dB)50.6 dB
Cut by 6 dB0.355 (-9.0 dB)0.00105 (-59.6 dB)50.6 dB

A second check after the cut shows the gap holding at 50.6 dB, because a level change moves signal and hiss together, so she gains 9 dB of headroom at no cost in clarity. Her next action is concrete: leave the dial at the second setting and record a 30-second clip with a playback check.

One caveat she keeps in mind: leave auto gain on and the browser raises the level during pauses, so the quiet reading looks better than it is. For a trustworthy reading, switch it off first, and trust the number only for this room, because a second voice or a closer desk changes it.

Microphone Test Troubleshooting for Low Volume and Clipping

When a test fails, the display usually shows why. Work through these troubleshooting fixes in order:

  • Unmute the device and raise its input slider in your mic settings.
  • Close Discord or any other app holding the hardware, then reload.
  • Update the driver or plug in again, and pick the correct microphone device.
  • Right-click the speaker icon in your taskbar, open the audio panel and confirm the right input is selected.
  • Check that your operating system lets the browser hear the webcam mic.

If the page works but your call audio does not, the fault sits inside that app's own settings, so check there next.

Fix Blocked Access Errors

A denied permission prompt is the most common cause. Click the lock icon, set the microphone to Allow, and use HTTPS, since browsers refuse access on insecure pages.

Distortion, Clipping and Flat Waveform

A flat line means no input, while a too quiet wave that barely moves means a weak source: move closer or lift the gain. A wave that slams the top shows clipping and harsh distortion, so back off. Sample reading on the tester's meter: a peak amplitude of 0.35 of full scale is 20 × log₁₀(0.35) ≈ -9.1 dB, comfortably under the 0 dB ceiling. A silent reading of 0.0016 gives -55.9 dB, leaving about 46.8 dB of headroom above the hiss. If the silent gap is the problem, speak up or mute the fan.

Echo Cancellation, Noise Suppression and Auto Gain

These browser filters help in calls but can thin your sound in a quality check. Turn them off in the advanced options for a raw reading, then restart your microphone.

Test Microphone Online in Chrome, Safari and Firefox

This mic tester works in any modern browser: Chrome, Safari, Firefox, Edge or Opera. A microphone test online relies on the getUserMedia request, so use HTTPS. It runs on Windows, Mac, Android, iOS and iPhone, on a laptop, desktop, mobile or tablet, and works with built-in or USB microphones. Want a second opinion? Use another online tester elsewhere, or repeat the microphone check after changing devices.

Microphone Test for Headsets in Discord, Zoom and Teams

A headset mic test confirms the boom is positioned well and the mute switch is off. Bluetooth and wireless models sometimes drop into hands-free mode with thinner sound, so test them here first and watch for delay. Test speaker output separately so a loud room does not feed back into the mic.

In Discord, open Voice & Video settings and press Let's Check; your voice plays back, and you are muted in the voice chat until you stop. Zoom, Teams and Meet each include an audio test, so try one before a meeting, an online class, gaming or a stream.

Private and Secure Microphone Testing in Your Browser

This test is secure by design: audio is processed locally in your browser, so no software is installed and nothing is sent out. That privacy matters, because a recorded clip can reveal a lot.

Microphone Quality Test With a Reference Microphone

For a deeper microphone quality test, use the tester's clip and playback to compare your mic with a reference microphone that has a known frequency response. Speak vocals at 30 cm, then move off-axis and listen for coloration; the off-axis response shows how it copes with a room. Up close, the proximity effect adds bass, so add a pop filter. A large-diaphragm condenser also picks up room tone, so repeat the take in a quiet studio. Use the result to pick the best microphone for your room.

faq_heading: Frequently Asked Questions About the Microphone Tester and How to Test Your Microphone

faq.q: Why does my browser say microphone access is blocked?
faq.a: The permission prompt was denied or the site was blocked earlier. Click the lock icon beside the address, set the microphone to Allow, then reload the page and press Start again.

faq.q: Why is the waveform flat during my mic test?
faq.a: A flat waveform means no signal is arriving. Choose another input device, unmute the microphone, raise the system input level and close any app, such as a call app, that is already using the device.

faq.q: What does the loopback option do?
faq.a: Loopback plays your microphone back through your speakers or headphones so you can hear delay and echo live. Use headphones, or the sound can feed back into the microphone.

faq.q: Does the test upload my voice?
faq.a: No. The audio is processed locally in your browser, and a recorded clip stays on your device until you download it as MP3 or WAV.

faq.q: Should I leave noise suppression, echo cancellation and auto gain on?
faq.a: They help in calls but can change how your voice sounds. Switch them off for a raw reading of your microphone, then restart the test so the browser applies the change.

faq.q: Why does my microphone work here but not in another app?
faq.a: The other app may be using a different input device, may be blocked by system privacy settings, or may be holding the device. Select the same microphone in that app's audio settings.

faq.q: What gain setting is best?
faq.a: Pick the lowest gain that keeps your voice clearly above background noise without the waveform hitting the top. A 0.5x setting is about -6 dB and 2x is about +6 dB.

content_blocks.html: Wondering what is plugged into your desk? This guide helps you show my mic details by walking through the label, connector and specifications that identify any microphone, so you can match your equipment to the types of microphones used for a podcast, a presentation or home recording. By the end you will know how to tell a dynamic mic from a condenser, read the sound pattern it picks up and decide whether it suits your audio needs.

Show My Mic: Find Out What Microphone You Have

Start with the obvious clues. Pick up your mic and look for a brand and model printed on the body, the base or the cable collar. A model name such as SM58 or AT2020 lets you look up the full spec sheet in seconds. If nothing is printed, check the sound settings on your computer: the operating system lists every audio input by name, and a USB device usually reports its own model there. Once you know the exact microphone, every later section of this guide becomes easy to apply to your own setup, whether you are chasing clean sound for recording or just a clearer voice on calls.

Check Your Built-in Microphone First

Many people already own a built-in microphone without realizing it. Laptops, cell phones, action cameras and mirrorless camera bodies all carry small built-in mics that convert sound to a signal for the headphones, the call app or the memory card. They work if that is all you have, but keep them about an arm's length away, since they offer little shielding against wind noise.

Check the XLR or USB Connector: Wired or Wireless

The connector tells you a great deal. A three-pin XLR plug points to a studio or stage mic that needs an interface or mixer, and often phantom power if it is a condenser. A USB plug means the mic carries its own converter and works straight from a computer. Look for a wired cable or a small wireless receiver, and a battery door that signals a transmitter. The round metal grille at the top hides the capsule, and its shape helps too: the ball-shaped head is why the microphone emoji looks the way it does. If you keep a whole microphone cabinet of gear, label each mic once identified so you never have to guess again.

How Microphones Work: From Sound Waves to Electric Signals

A microphone is a transducer: it turns the pressure of sound waves into electric signals that an amplifier can boost. Sound reaches a thin diaphragm that vibrates, and the way each mic turns that vibration into voltage defines its character. This matters because the same voice or guitar sounds very different through two designs. Understanding that single step, shared by modern microphones and vintage ones, explains why rugged stage microphones, delicate studio microphones and tiny clip-on units all behave differently, and why the audio you capture depends on the sound source as much as the gear.

Types of Microphones: Dynamic, Condenser and Ribbon

Most microphones fall into three families, and finding which microphone type you own narrows down everything else. Each suits a different job, and a well-stocked mic locker usually includes all three. The four short sections below cover them and the specialized microphones that grew out of them.

Dynamic Mics for Loud Sources

A dynamic microphone pairs a diaphragm with a coil and magnet, which makes it rugged and reliable. A dynamic mic handles loud guitar amps and drums, shrugs off handling noise and rejects background noise better than most condensers. It has lower sensitivity, so hold it close to the source. Strong professional mics are available at a modest price, and these mics last for years.

Condenser Mics for Detail

A condenser microphone is more sensitive and captures high-fidelity detail, which is why it dominates the recording studio. A condenser mic comes as a large-diaphragm design, popular for vocals, or a small-diaphragm pencil condenser, preferred for sources with fast transients. The catch is that it also hears everything else. In an untreated room a condenser microphone can pick up reflections, and some budget models sound a little sibilant. Perfect for a quiet podcast recording corner, less so for a noisy kitchen.

Ribbon Mics and Their Velvety Sound

A ribbon microphone uses a thin metal strip and is famous for a smooth, velvety tone. A ribbon mic once needed careful handling because vintage versions were delicate, but modern mics are sturdier and more versatile. Engineers and musician friends often reach for one to soften harsh sources.

Specialized Shotgun, Lavalier and Stereo Mics

A shotgun microphone has a narrow pickup, ideal for dialogue on a set with a boom pole or a camera mount. A lavalier microphone clips to clothing and connects to a wireless microphone receiver, which suits presenters and every vlog or interview. A stereo microphone records two channels at once for ambience. Speakerphone units pack several capsules around a table, and a kick drum mic is tuned for low-end punch. Prices for the content creator range wildly, from cheap clip-ons to professional film rigs, and filmmaker kits often combine all three.

Reading the Polar Pattern of Your Mic

The polar pattern describes the directions your mic hears best. It is one of the quickest ways to place an unknown microphone, because manufacturers print the symbol on the body or the box, and most microphones sold for recording follow the same few symbols. The same pickup pattern drives how much room sound reaches the capsule, so it affects recording quality and how a band, a singer or a speaker will sound at home.

Cardioid: The Common Pickup Pattern

Cardioid is the most common choice. It hears the front, rejects the sides and back, and keeps background noise down. A single cardioid mic is the safe pick for a speaker or singer, and most dynamic mics use it. If you only remember one pattern, remember cardioid.

Omnidirectional for Ambient Sound

An omnidirectional mic hears equally from every side. Omni mics capture the whole room, which suits group recordings and field ambience, but it also invites unwanted sound from anywhere.

Figure-8 for Face-to-Face Interviews

A figure-8 pattern picks up the front and the back while ignoring the sides, so one mic placed between two people records both sides of an interview cleanly.

Multi-pattern and Shotgun Lobar Mics

Some designs let you switch patterns, useful for mixing a studio session where the sound source changes. Shotgun and lobar mics narrow the pickup further, but they bring a slight sensitivity to the proximity effect and off-axis coloration, so check the performance you need before buying.

Mic Specifications That Help You Identify a Microphone

Numbers on a spec sheet look scary, yet a handful of specifications do most of the work when you want to confirm which mic you really own. Each one maps to something you can hear.

SPL Rating and Sound Pressure Level

The SPL figure shows how much sound pressure level the mic can take before it distorts. A singer who hits a loud chorus can overload a sensitive mic, so a high rating means safer capture of loud sources. Pair it with the self-noise, or noise floor, and you get the dynamic range, the gap between the quietest and loudest audio quality the mic can record.

Capsule and Diaphragm Design

The capsule holds the diaphragm, and its size and material shape the sound waves it can follow. Some makers sputter gold onto the diaphragm to keep it thin and even. Bigger capsules tend to sound fuller; smaller ones react faster.

Frequency Response Curve

A frequency response chart shows which pitches get boosted or cut. A bump in the upper mid range adds presence to a voice, while a flat curve stays neutral. Compare the curve printed in the manual with the way your vocals actually sound to confirm the model.

Bass Roll-off and Highpass Filter

A switch marked bass roll-off, sometimes called a highpass filter, trims low rumble. It also tames the proximity effect, the bass boost you get when you speak very close to a directional mic. Its presence is another clue that you hold a studio or broadcast model.

Identifying an Unlabeled Mic: One Desk Drawer Case

I want a clean voice track for a recorded talk, and the only candidate is a black, unmarked mic from the back of a drawer. Which microphone is this, and will it do the job? The answer, as it turns out, is a condenser I can name and place at about 5 cm from my mouth.

First, the clues. The body has a three-pin XLR output and no battery door, so it is wired and needs power from the interface. Under the grille sits a large capsule. Engraved on the underside, almost worn away, I can read "AT2020". I look up the published sheet: cardioid, 144 dB maximum SPL, 20 dB self-noise, and 48 V phantom power (the IEC 61938 standard). Plugging it into an interface with phantom power switched on confirms it: the meter lights up, and with the switch off it stays silent.

Now that I know which mic this is, I check that its specs suit speech. The dynamic range is 144 − 20 = 124 dB, far more than speech needs. What matters is how far my voice sits above the 20 dB noise floor. Speech runs roughly 60 dB SPL at 1 m, and level rises 6 dB each time the distance halves:

  • At 20 cm: 60 + 20 × log10(100 / 20) = 74 dB, which is 54 dB above the noise floor.
  • At 10 cm: 80 dB, which is 60 dB above it.
  • At 5 cm: 86 dB, which is 66 dB above it.

Now that the mic is identified, the number to watch is distance, not the dynamic range. Moving from 20 cm to 5 cm buys 12 dB of extra signal for free, and I recompute by hand with 20 × log10(20 / 5) = 12.04 dB to cross-check the table. I settle on 10 cm as a compromise, because at 5 cm plosives and the proximity effect start to boom.

One edge case when you trust a spec sheet for the mic you have: the 20 dB self-noise figure flatters this mic in my spare room. The room itself sits near 35 dB, so the room, not the capsule, sets the limit, and a lower self-noise model would sound no cleaner. So the identified AT2020 stays, and a test take at 10 cm tells me the rest.

Common Studio Mics You Might Recognize

Most professional studio rooms rely on roughly the same handful of microphones. If yours is one of them, an engineer can tell you how it is normally used. A few appear in nearly every mic locker, and each has its own sweet spot.

Shure SM57 and Shure SM58 Workhorses

The Shure SM57 sets the standard for snare drum and guitar cabinets, and the Shure SM58 is the classic live vocal tool. Their internal parts are similar, and the main difference is the grille, which is why the microphone emoji copies the SM58 shape. Both handle loud transients with ease.

Shure SM7B and Electro-Voice RE20 for Voice

The Shure SM7B and the Electro-Voice RE20 are dynamic favorites for podcasting and broadcast voice. They stay smooth on aggressive vocals, and many recording engineers prefer them over condensers in an imperfect room.

Kick Drum Mics from AKG and Sennheiser

A drummer needs low-end punch, so models such as the AKG D112, Shure Beta 52A and Sennheiser MD421 are tuned for kick drum recording and toms. If your mic has a shaped, boosted response in the lows, it probably belongs to this group.

Neumann, AKG and Royer Studio Classics

Premium condenser microphones and ribbons, from the Neumann U87 to the AKG C414 and Royer 121, are the prestige tier. Their high-fidelity sound comes with a big price, though affordable entry models such as the Blue Yeti give a taste of the same idea for desk use.

Find the Right Microphone for Your Needs

Once you know what you have, you can judge whether it fits the task. Several guides about how to find the right microphone agree on one theme: match the mic to your room, your voice and your use, and never expect fixing in the mix to rescue a wrong choice. Plan to select the perfect microphone for the job first, then fine-tune it. Try a few options if you can, because every voice and every room differs.

Pick a Vocal Mic for Podcast and Home Studio

For a vocal mic in a home studio, a good dynamic often beats a condenser at the same price. Dynamics hear less of the room, so an untreated space with no acoustic treatment suffers less. Choose the right mic for your voice, and if you chase a bright, airy podcast sound, remember that a darker mic is safer when in doubt. If you choose the right mic and the wrong room, the band or voice will still sound thin, so treat the space too.

Choose a Mic for Conference Room, Classroom and PA System

For a presentation in a meeting room, conference microphones such as a speakerphone or ceiling array keeps audio even around a table. In a classroom or a PA system, a handheld or headset unit keeps the mouth close to the capsule and the sound clear.

Live Performance Venue Mics

If the mic you identified is a handheld dynamic like the SM58, it already suits the stage. A wired handheld is the simple pick, while a wireless setup frees movement during a live performance, so charge the batteries before the doors open.

On a Budget? Use What You Have

A smaller budget does not mean poor results. Many affordable dynamic microphones hold up well, and a camera or phone placed closer to the source can beat an expensive mic placed too far away. Check what mic you already own, keep it near your mouth, and ask the find the right mic questions above before spending more.

faq_heading: Show My Microphone — Frequently Asked Questions

faq.q: Why does my browser show the wrong microphone?
faq.a: Browsers default to the system's "Default Input Device" setting, not necessarily the last microphone you plugged in. To check which one the browser is using, open your OS sound settings (Windows: Sound → Input; macOS: System Settings → Sound → Input) and confirm which device is set as the default. After changing it, refresh this page — the device list will update to reflect the new default at the top of the selection order.

faq.q: What does it mean if my microphone name shows as "Default" or a partial ID?
faq.a: This usually means the browser hasn't been granted full microphone permission yet, or your browser version limits device label exposure for privacy reasons. Click Allow on the permission prompt to unlock full device names and specifications. In Firefox, you may need to select "Remember this decision" to retain access across sessions. In Brave or Safari, device enumeration may be partially restricted even with permission granted.

faq.q: Can this tool identify my exact microphone model?
faq.a: The tool reads exactly what your browser's MediaDevices API reports, which comes from your operating system's audio driver registration. If your OS has the correct driver installed, you'll see the full product name. If the driver is generic or the device uses a shared USB audio class driver, the name may be a chipset or class identifier rather than a brand name. To confirm the exact model, check Device Manager (Windows) or System Information (macOS) for the full hardware descriptor.

faq.q: My microphone has a "Fair" or "Basic" quality rating — what should I check?
faq.a: The quality rating is calculated from five factors: sample rate, sample size, channel count, latency, and whether audio processing features are active. A low rating most often means your sample rate is below 44.1 kHz, your sample size is 8-bit, or your mic is operating in a degraded mode (e.g. via a heavily compressed Bluetooth connection). Check your OS audio settings to ensure the device isn't forced into a telephony mode (8 kHz or 16 kHz). For Bluetooth mics, switching the device out of "hands-free" mode into a higher-quality audio profile can significantly improve the rating.

How to Record Your Voice Online in Your Browser

Here is how to use this recorder to record audio: press start recording and speak. The level meter, elapsed timer and live waveform show your sound and speech reaching the recording tool, and the voice recorder works on a computer, smartphone or any other device with a microphone.

Allow Microphone Access First

When the permission dialog appears, allow microphone access. If you blocked it earlier, click the icon in the address bar and choose Allow in Chrome or Firefox, then check the Windows or macOS settings. Pick another microphone from the dropdown if you have several, and lower the volume or echo if the level clips.

Pause and Resume, Then Stop Recording

Step one is to speak at a steady distance. Use pause and resume whenever you need a breath, and hit stop recording when the take is done. Each pause keeps the same recording instead of starting a new file.

Preview, Then Download MP3

Preview the take, then export it. Press download to save the MP3 on your device; the export happens locally in your browser, so the MP3 file is ready in seconds.

Why This Free Voice Recorder Works for Everyone

A free voice recorder should not ask for an account or a sign-up. This one is free, and the high-quality sound suits interviews, dictation, singing, music or video narration. Podcasts start the same way: record a clean take with this tool and download it for your host, so listeners get the episode through an RSS feed.

Privacy and Local Processing

Your privacy is protected because the audio stays local to the browser. Nothing reaches our servers, so there is no storage to secure or encrypted upload to worry about; close the tab and the working copy disappears.

Podcast-Ready MP3 at 128 kbps

This recorder exports an MP3 at a 128 kbps bitrate, a podcast standard that weighs about 0.96 MB per minute. A WAV file is far bigger. Normalize loudness in your editor if the platform you publish to asks for it.

Voice Recording Cleanup and Audio Editor Tools

A short voice recording rarely needs a full audio editor. Basic editing covers the cleanup most takes need: use noise reduction against background noise, then edit and trim the ends before you share it. An app is optional.

Silence Trimming Cuts Dead Air

Silence trimming in this recorder removes the quiet gaps at the start and end of your take, so you trim less by hand.

Crop Takes with an Audio Trimmer

An audio trimmer crops the recorded take to the part you want before download. Trim, preview again and export.

Sizing a 17-Minute Interview with the Online Mic Recorder

I have a 17 minute 40 second interview to email to an editor, and the question is whether the file will fit. I open the online voice recorder, allow the microphone, and keep my peaks near -9 dB on the meter, the middle of the target zone above. The export lands as a 128 kbps MP3.

The size comes straight from the bitrate: 128,000 bits per second is 16,000 bytes per second, and 1,060 seconds of audio gives 16.96 MB. That sits under Gmail's 25 MB attachment limit, so the decision is simple: attach it directly rather than upload it somewhere.

The sensitivity rerun is the useful part. At 192 kbps the same take weighs 25.44 MB, over the limit before any email overhead. Email also encodes attachments with base64, which adds about a third, so the 25 MB cap fits roughly 18.75 MB of raw audio: at the recorder's 128 kbps export, about 19 minutes 32 seconds. The elapsed timer read 17:40, so the take clears it by under two minutes.

My judgement call: the length matters more than the bitrate here. A second interview running 22 minutes would need a share link or a trim first, since speech at 128 kbps already sounds clean. I recomputed the 1,060-second figure by hand from the timer to confirm it before sending.

Transcribe an Audio Recording to Text

To transcribe a take, export the MP3 and run it through speech to text. That transcription gives you text transcripts, and a subtitle or caption file is built from them. The speech recorder itself only captures sound.

Share a Link or Embed Your Voice Notes

Once the file is exported, share a link to it or embed the voice notes in a page. Keep the audio on your side until you choose to publish.

Fix Online Mic Recorder Problems

If the online voice recorder stays silent, treat it like any audio recorder or voice memo app and confirm the browser has the right input selected. Watch the maximum record time and recording length too: a long take means a bigger file.

How to Use This Sound Level Meter Online

Three steps get you a result with this online sound level meter: allow the microphone, watch the gauge, then adjust the settings if you want a different view of the sound.

Allow Microphone Access

Press start and approve the permission prompt. Your phone, laptop or computer then streams audio to the page, and nothing is uploaded. The same steps work in a mobile browser, so the device in your pocket is enough.

Read the Real-Time Noise Level, Min, Max and Average

The large gauge shows the current reading, while min, max and the average level summarise the session. Hold the device still for about 30 seconds and trust the average level over one brief peak, because real sound keeps shifting.

Choose dBA Frequency Weighting and Peak Hold

Frequency weighting decides which pitches count most. Pick dBA for everyday noise, since the A-weighted curve follows human hearing; dBC (C-weighted) keeps more bass, and dBZ is flat. Peak hold freezes the highest level so you catch a clap. Choose fast or slow response, watch for clipping, and read LAeq as the steady equivalent level.

Use the History and Spectrum Graphs

The history chart plots the last 30 seconds, so you can see when a level rose. The frequency spectrum shows which frequency ranges carry the energy. Set warning thresholds, for example amber at 70 dBA and red at 85 dBA, and note that some tools report LUFS for audio loudness instead.

Reference Sound Levels for Your Loudness Meter

Checking a Café Grinder Station with a Sound Level Meter Online

Marguerite runs a small café and wants to know whether the espresso grinder corner needs hearing protection for her two baristas, who each stand there about five hours a day. She opens the sound level meter on a phone, sets dBA, clears the history and holds the phone at ear height, 40 cm from the grinder, for a full 60 seconds of steady milling.

The gauge settles around 87 dBA, and the session summary reads an average of 87.4 dBA with a peak near 96 dBA. She trusts the average, not the peak, because a daily limit is about sustained level. Running the 3 dB rule by hand gives T = 8 / 2(87.4-85)/3 ≈ 4.59 hours, or 4 h 36 min. That is shorter than a five-hour shift, so this reading overshoots the NIOSH 85 dBA recommendation by about 24 minutes a day.

The number to watch is the 2 dB uncertainty. A phone microphone with automatic gain control can easily sit that far from a calibrated instrument, and as the second row shows, a 2 dB error moves the allowed time by almost two hours. So the result here is a screening answer, not proof. My judgement call: since even the lower figure fails, she rotates the baristas off the grinder every two hours and prices a four-decibel enclosure. If a dispute or an inspection ever depends on the number, a calibrated Class 2 meter is the instrument to use instead of this page.

Sound Meter Accuracy and Calibration

An online sound meter gives an estimate, not a lab result: its accuracy is limited until it is matched to a calibrated source. Treat it as an uncalibrated screening aid rather than a Class 1 instrument from a professional supplier, and never use it for regulatory compliance.

dB SPL vs dBFS: What Your Reading Means

Microphones record digital level (dBFS), where 0 is the maximum. A true dB SPL figure measures air pressure and needs a calibrated microphone and a standard. Until then, compare readings with each other, not with a legal limit. Reported in dBA, the number still reflects your own microphone.

Calibration Offset and a Reference Meter

Play a steady 1kHz sine tone from a tone generator through a speaker at a fixed volume. Hold a reference meter, such as an SPL meter, beside the device and enter the difference as the calibration offset. A calibrator producing 94 dB makes that tone exact. Calibration of headphones follows the same logic.

Common Sources of Error

Phones apply automatic gain control and noise suppression, which flatten loud events, so switch them off where you can. Background noise, the distance to the source and a reflective room all shift a reading, and each microphone and device differs, so a sound meter on one phone can disagree with another. Note your distance, repeat the check three times and keep a short report of the averages.

Online Decibel Meter Readings and Safe Exposure Time

Loudness matters for your hearing, health and safety because harm depends on both level and exposure. Any sound decibel meter reading above 85 dBA starts the clock on safe exposure, and the exposure time shrinks quickly as the level climbs.

The 3 dB Exchange Rate and NIOSH Limits

The 3 dB exchange rate used by NIOSH, part of the CDC, halves the allowed time for every 3 dB above 85 dBA, and the WHO also warns about noise exposure. Keep safe noise levels below 85 dBA over a full day. With level L in dBA, the allowed time in hours is:

T = 8 / (2(L-85)/3)

Worked Example: A Workshop Reading

A woodworker's planer reads 91.5 dBA at ear height, so T = 8 / 2(91.5-85)/3 ≈ 1.78 hours, about 1 h 47 min of unprotected work. Each 3 dB shift halves or doubles that figure:

Hearing Loss, Tinnitus and Hearing Protection

Loud noise bruises the hair cells of the inner ear, causing noise-induced hearing loss that never heals, plus tinnitus. The hearing damage risk grows with level, so wear hearing protection above 85 dBA. Chronic noise pollution also raises stress and disturbs sleep, so treat a sustained meter average above 85 dBA as your cue to act on your health.

Noise Meter Online: Uses at Home and Work

People use an online noise meter to check the environment around them, from a noisy neighbour to a white noise machine.

Bedroom and Sleep Checks

At home, measure the bedroom at night: under about 35 dBA suits sleep. Once the meter confirms a quiet room below 40 dBA, it also suits an online hearing test.

Workplace Noise Checks

In a shared office or workplace, run the meter for the loudest hour and note the average dBA to find the source before it adds stress or hurts concentration.

How Your Browser Measures Sound Pressure Level

The page asks the browser for the microphone, turns loudness in the audio stream into digital samples and shows the result as a number, so it behaves like a software loudness meter built on a sound pressure level estimate.

FFT, RMS and Decibel Mapping

An FFT splits the signal into bands of frequency for weighting, then RMS averages the signal power before it is mapped to a decibel value with the calibration offset.

Privacy: Nothing Leaves Your Browser

All audio is analysed on your device and discarded. Because nothing is uploaded, your privacy stays intact and no report of your room is stored on a server.

content_blocks.html: Speak into the voice frequency analyzer and your voice becomes a live frequency spectrum, with your pitch in Hz updating in real time. This free tool is built for speech, so within seconds you can read your fundamental frequency, see your harmonics and judge the tonal balance of your voice.

How to Use the Voice Frequency Analyzer

  1. Click Start and allow microphone access when your browser asks.
  2. Hold a steady vowel such as "ahh" for two to three seconds, then talk in your normal speaking voice.
  3. Read the peak on the graph: the tallest bar is your pitch, and smaller bars to its right are harmonics.
  4. Switch between bars and a line view; the line makes narrow peaks easier to spot, and the spectrogram shows change over time.
  5. Try a whisper as well. Consonants such as "s" and "sh" push energy higher, while a vowel keeps it low, and unvoiced sounds carry no pitch at all.

Keep the microphone a hand's width from your mouth for clean audio, pause during silence, since a noise gate removes background input from the reading, and use a quiet room so ordinary noise does not tilt the result.

Voice Frequency Analysis: Reading Your Results

A voice frequency analysis is a quick voice analysis, not a diagnosis, and it answers one question: which frequencies carry the energy in this sample, and where does the loudest pitch sit? Unvoiced sounds are excluded, so only voiced moments count.

Fundamental Frequency and Your Speaking Pitch

The fundamental frequency (F0) is how many times per second your vocal folds open and close, measured in hertz. Say you hold "ahh" and the display settles at 137 Hz: your vocal cords vibrate 137 times each second. The nearest musical note is C#3 at 138.59 Hz, so your voice pitch is about 20 cents flat. A doubling of frequency is one octave, so 274 Hz would sit exactly an octave up.

cents = 1200 × log₂(f / (fnote))

Harmonics, Overtones and Tonal Character

Harmonics are whole-number multiples of F0: a 137 Hz tone has harmonics at 274, 411 and 548 Hz. These overtones shape the tonal character you hear. The vocal tract boosts some of them, forming formants, and that resonance is why a warm voice and a bright voice differ even at equal pitch. On the graph they appear as evenly spaced peaks that shrink toward the right, like the waveform's finer detail.

f_n = n × F_0

Median, Mean and Typical Range of a Sample

Read the median first: it is the middle value of the sample and ignores stray spikes. The mean averages every reading, so a few high values drag it up. The typical range runs from the 10th to the 90th percentile; if yours spans 137 to 184 Hz, the spread is 12 × log2(184 ÷ 137) ≈ 5.1 semitones (one semitone is a twelfth of an octave). The median also stays put when you cough. Good pitch accuracy shows as a narrow band, while a slow upward or downward slide signals pitch drift. Compare only samples taken the same way.

Checking a Podcast Microphone with the Voice Frequency Analyzer

I'm recording a podcast intro and want to know whether my voice pitch stays consistent between a seated take and a standing take, because the editor says the second one sounds "brighter". I open the analyzer, read the passage aloud for 15 seconds each time, and note the median rather than the mean, since one cough would skew an average.

Take one, seated, gives a median of 118.4 Hz. That sits comfortably inside the 85–180 Hz range usually quoted for adult men, and the nearest note is A#2 at 116.54 Hz, so I'm about 27 cents sharp of it. Take two, standing, returns 131.9 Hz. The voice frequency analysis tells me the gap is 13.5 Hz, which is 12 × log2(131.9 ÷ 118.4) ≈ 1.87 semitones, a rise of about 11%.

For the sensitivity rerun I change one input: the microphone distance. Moving the capsule 15 cm further away drops the median to 126.7 Hz, so about 0.7 semitone of the "brightness" was my posture and the rest was how the microphone and my voice interact, not a new voice. What stands out is that the number to watch is the median across takes, not one peak.

The trap is the octave error: 2 × 118.4 = 236.8 Hz. If the display jumps to 236.8 Hz, the detector has locked onto the second harmonic, and that reading would wrongly land in the typical female range. A jump of exactly twelve semitones is the giveaway, so I repeat the take instead of trusting it, because a spike like that should never be averaged in. My decision: record the final take standing, with the microphone 15 cm further back, and rerun the analyzer once more to confirm the median stays near 127 Hz.

Frequency Spectrum Bands: Bass, Mid, Presence, Brilliance

The analyzer splits the sound into four frequency bands, using an FFT, so you can see where your audio signal is strong or thin. Each band is measured in dB and in kHz terms at its upper edge.

BandRangeWhat it adds
Bass80–300 HzBody and depth; too much sounds boomy
Mid300 Hz–2 kHzIntelligibility: vowels and warmth
Presence2–4 kHzForward clarity and loudness cut
Brilliance4 kHz and upAir and sibilance, the crisp edge of "s"

When you open the analyzer before speaking, a spike at 50 or 60 Hz lands in the bass band and is mains hum, not your voice, so check for it when the low end looks strong; a spike 10 dB above its neighbours is typical. A flat brilliance band tells you the sound is dull.

Dominant Frequency and the Spectrogram View

The dominant frequency is the single strongest bin in the spectrum, and the spectrogram plots it over time so you can watch it move as you speak.

Voice Pitch Ranges by Voice Type

Your voice type depends on vocal fold length and mass, so there is no correct number; the ranges below are common patterns for singing and speech.

Speaking Frequency for Adult Men and Women

Adult men usually speak between 85 and 180 Hz, a deep bass near 85–100 Hz and a tenor near 150–180 Hz, with a baritone between them. Adult women usually speak between 165 and 255 Hz, from alto near 165–190 Hz to soprano near 220–260 Hz. The male and female ranges overlap around 150–200 Hz, so pitch alone cannot name a speaker as male or female.

How Voice Frequency Changes with Age

Before puberty most voices sit near 250–300 Hz. The larynx then grows and male pitch drops sharply, female pitch only a little. A child's reading near 250–300 Hz is normal on the analyzer, and your vocal range for singing is a separate measure.

Practical Uses for a Sound Spectrum Analyzer

The analyzer's spectrum view works as an audio spectrum analyzer for room acoustics and any music or recording where you cannot hear what is wrong with your voice. Play a sine wave or pink noise and watch how your room changes it.

Fixing Thin Sound on Video Calls

If you sound tinny on video calls or a conference call, speak into the analyzer and compare the bands. A weak mid band means your microphone or its position is cutting your voice. A missing presence band is common with laptop microphones. A dominant bass band points to proximity effect, and a dip near 1–3 kHz suggests comb filtering from a reflective desk.

Vocal Training and Pitch Monitoring

Singers and vocal coaches hold a note and watch the Hz readout: it should stay steady. The tuner view shows the closest musical note against A4 = 440 Hz, a standard tuning reference, so note detection tells you how many cents you are off. A held note and plain speech are different samples, so label them separately.

Limits of a Pitch Detector and Voice Checker

A poor microphone adds noise that can distort the analyzer's reading. A pitch detector can mistake a strong harmonic for F0 and report a result an octave too high. If a reading suddenly doubles, repeat the sound. Breathy or very quiet speech may give no reading, and the voice band for telephone speech is far narrower than this view.

  • Run each voice frequency test, voice hz test or voice pitch test with one clear sound and the same microphone, and compare the median across takes.
  • Do not treat one result as who you are; a voice checker measures a sample, not identity or health.
  • Save readings to CSV and repeat before judging any change.

faq_heading: Voice Frequency Analyzer — Frequently Asked Questions

faq.q: What is a normal voice frequency for speaking?
faq.a: Adult men typically speak at 85–180 Hz (average: ~120 Hz); adult women at 165–255 Hz (average: ~210 Hz). There is no "correct" speaking frequency — it is determined by the length and mass of your vocal folds, which are set by genetics. However, habitual pitch can be consciously raised or lowered with training, and many people unconsciously shift their speaking pitch depending on context (formal vs casual, authoritative vs empathetic).

faq.q: Why does my fundamental frequency change throughout the day?
faq.a: Voice frequency is influenced by hydration, muscle warm-up, and hormonal cycles. Immediately after waking, vocal folds are less hydrated and the voice typically runs 5–15 Hz lower than usual. After speaking for 10–15 minutes, folds warm up and frequency stabilises. Dehydration throughout the day causes progressive stiffening that raises the fundamental frequency slightly. Menstrual cycle hormones in women can cause measurable frequency shifts. Stress increases laryngeal muscle tension, which raises pitch.

faq.q: Can I use the voice frequency analyzer to tune my singing voice?
faq.a: Yes — sustain a note, read the fundamental frequency in Hz, and compare it to the target note frequency (A4 = 440 Hz, C4 = 261.6 Hz, etc.). The "Closest Note" display and cents deviation reading show you how close to the target pitch you are. However, for dedicated pitch training, a chromatic tuner designed for vocal use gives more musical feedback. This voice frequency analyzer is more useful for understanding the full spectral character of your voice than for precise pitch-by-pitch tuning exercises.

faq.q: Why is my fundamental frequency display showing "--" or fluctuating wildly?
faq.a: The analyzer needs a sustained, tonal sound to detect a clear fundamental frequency. Background noise, consonants, whispers, and ambient room sounds produce complex, atonal spectra where pitch detection algorithms struggle to identify a single dominant frequency. Sustain a clear "ahhh" vowel and hold it steady for 2–3 seconds to get a stable reading. Also check that the room is reasonably quiet — constant noise above 60 dB can swamp the microphone signal and make pitch detection unreliable.

faq.q: What do the Hz numbers mean for my voice quality?
faq.a: The Hz value on its own does not indicate voice quality — it only indicates pitch. A deep voice at 100 Hz is not better or worse than a higher voice at 220 Hz. What matters for voice quality is the distribution of frequency energy: a well-balanced voice with strong presence (2–4 kHz) is clear and intelligible; a voice with weak mids is muffled; one with excessive bass is boomy. Use the frequency distribution bands below the spectrum graph to assess quality, not just the fundamental frequency reading.

The free online noise analyzer listens through your microphone in your browser, needs no registration, and shows your overall noise level in dBFS plus how the sound splits across frequency bands, so you get a clear baseline measurement of the audio in your environment.

How to Use the Background Noise Analyzer

The online background noise test runs on the Web Audio API and getUserMedia, so your microphone audio is analyzed on your device only.

  1. Pick your microphone and set the sample duration.
  2. Keep speech out of the sample and stay quiet in your usual environment.
  3. Read the result, change one thing and compare it against your baseline.

Start the Test and Allow Microphone Access

Press start, then allow microphone access when your browser asks. If nothing happens, close Zoom or any other app holding the mic and retry. The history log keeps each run, and a threshold alert flags a noisy space.

Stay Quiet During the Sample

A short run suits steady noise such as a fan; a longer one catches intermittent noise, though it cannot promise a passing truck shows up. Privacy note: nothing is uploaded.

Read Your Ambient Noise Level

The average summarizes your ambient noise over the run, while peak, minimum and maximum show how much the levels moved. Your background noise level is only trustworthy next to another run from the same mic, because an uncalibrated meter shows relative digital full-scale values, not sound pressure level.

Leq, L10 and L90 Explained

Leq is the energy average of your noise measurement. L10 is the level exceeded 10% of the time (the peaks) and L90 the level exceeded 90% of the time, which approximates the quiet floor. A big gap between them means conditions keep changing.

Decibel Reference Chart for Common Sounds

If you use a calibrated decibel meter or sound meter, dBA and dB SPL readings fall roughly here, which also tells you whether a space is suitable for sleep, a home office or a workshop.

Level (dBA)Typical soundHow it feels

Frequency Spectrum and Room Noise

The frequency spectrum of your audio shows what the room noise is made of. The spectrum analyzer view, with a frequency analyzer readout of the dominant frequency in hertz and a spectrogram over time, helps you trace a problem back to its source instead of guessing.

Frequency Bands: Low, Mid and High

Bass and sub bass sit in the low band, speech in the mid band, and treble in the high band. If one share jumps after you fix something, check the overall level too, since percentages shift when another component drops.

Electrical Hum and Low-Frequency Rumble

A spike near 50 or 60 Hz suggests mains hum from wiring or a transformer, and its harmonics repeat above it. Rumble from HVAC, air conditioning or traffic piles up in the same low band, while hiss lives in the high band.

Octave Bands and A-Weighting

Octave bands group the spectrum in proportional steps; white noise and pink noise are the usual test signals. A-weighting trims bass and treble to mimic your ear, so a weighting choice changes the number you read.

Noise Floor vs Microphone Noise

Your noise floor is the quietest level your setup can show. It includes microphone noise (self-noise), input gain and mic gain choices, and any clipping, so the lowest reading is not always the space's true acoustic level. Keep gain fixed when you compare. Make a ten-second recording with your usual microphone, then repeat with the gain halved; if the audio floor barely moves, the microphone noise, not your space, sets the limit. A noise floor analyzer works the same way.

Common Types of Background Noise

Fans and appliances give a steady noise source that shows as a flat band of energy, mains hum is a narrow spike near 50 or 60 Hz, and hiss lifts the high band. Clicks and interference appear as sudden peaks, and artifacts add acoustic problems that the room tone itself does not explain.

Signal-to-Noise Ratio Guidelines

SNR is your talker level minus the floor. For example, a talker at -18 dB over a floor of -61 dB gives 43 dB:

CaseFloor levelSNR (dB)

Directional mic, treated booth-6850

Calibrate Your Background Noise Test

Calibration ties dBFS to a real sound pressure level. Match a trusted reference meter during steady sound at the same position and weighting, then save the offset for that microphone. Say the reference meter reads 38.0 dBA while the page shows -57.0 on its digital scale: the calibration offset is +95.0 dB for that microphone, weighting and gain. A later reading of -49.0 then corresponds to roughly 46 dBA. Repeat your background noise level test whenever the audio interface, gain or position changes, because that calibration no longer applies; without it, compare runs only against each other.

The 10 dB Rule Explained

The 10 dB rule says ambient sound should sit at least 10 dB below what you measure. A source at 60 dB needs a room at 50 dB or lower for accuracy within about 0.5 dB.

Match a Reference Meter and Export the Data

Export the CSV after each calibrated run so podcasting or studio sessions stay documented.

Spare-Room Noise Measurement: Window Open vs Closed

Dana opens the analyzer to check whether her spare room, a planned voice-over booth, stays under 35 dBA, the ANSI/ASA S12.60 classroom limit and a fair yardstick for speech work.

She first calibrates against a handheld meter that reads 36.9 dBA while the page shows -54.4 dBFS, giving an offset of 36.9 + 54.4 = +91.3 dB for this microphone, gain and A-weighting. Then she runs the analyzer for two 60-second samples, changing only the window.

WindowLeq (dBFS)Calibrated (dBA)SNR for speech at -21.5 dBFS
Open-50.241.128.7 dB
Closed-57.933.436.4 dB

The closed-window result of 33.4 dBA clears the 35 dBA target by 1.6 dB, while the open window misses it by 6.1 dB. Closing the window removes 7.7 dB of street noise, and that is the number to watch: it moves the signal-to-noise ratio from 28.7 dB to 36.4 dB. She cross-checks by hand, adding the offset to each reading, and both match the meter's trend.

The edge case is the refrigerator in the next room. Its compressor cycles, so a 60-second Leq can land in a quiet stretch and flatter the room. Dana's L10 sits well above her L90, which tells her the floor is not steady, so she repeats the run for five minutes before trusting 33.4. Her offset also only holds at this gain: touching the input level by even 6 dB shifts every calibrated figure, so she tapes the gain knob in place. Her next action is a fresh five-minute closed-window run, then a draught strip for the window frame.

Noise Reduction Fixes for Ambient Sound

Start with the source of the audio problem, rerun the analyzer after every change to compare against your baseline, then use noise reduction software only for what remains. Heavy processing adds artifacts, so a gentle noise gate beats aggressive cleanup.

  • If the low band dominates, switch off the heater, move away from appliances and rerun.
  • Put a headset or directional mic close to your voice for better audio.
  • Add acoustic treatment to cut reverb in a recording room.

Noise Suppression and Auto Gain Control

Noise suppression in meeting apps hides steady background noise, but it answers a different question from measuring the room. Switch off auto gain control and echo cancellation for the test, since they move the numbers.

Fix Fans, Hiss and Echo

A fan shows as a steady low-band level and hiss as high-band energy. Lower the input gain to cut noise at the source, then confirm in the analyzer that the level dropped; soft panels soften reflections.

Room Tone Checks Before Calls and Recordings

Run a check before video calls, meetings or a podcast, and again after you change speaker position or move to a quiet room. Audio quality depends on your environment as much as your microphone, so test the same environment you will use for recording, at the hour you will use it.

Is Your Audio Recorded?

No. Measurement happens in your browser, so no audio recording is saved or sent, and you can revoke microphone permission at any time.

faq.q: What is a good background noise level for recording?
faq.a: Many home recording setups aim for a calibrated room level around 35 dBA or lower and a signal-to-noise ratio of at least 40 dB, so your voice sits well above the floor.

faq.q: Is this an absolute decibel meter?
faq.a: Not by itself. A browser reads relative digital levels in dBFS. Matching a trusted reference meter gives an offset that converts the reading to an estimated dBA for that microphone, gain and weighting.

faq.q: What is the 10 dB rule for background noise?
faq.a: For a measurement to be accurate within about 0.5 dB, the background must sit at least 10 dB below the source you measure. This calculator checks that gap from your two levels.

faq.q: Why does my noise reading change between runs?
faq.a: Fans, air conditioning, keyboard clicks, passing traffic and automatic gain control all move the level. Take several samples with one change at a time and compare them.

faq.q: Which sample duration should I choose?
faq.a: Ten seconds suits steady noise; 30 to 60 seconds gives intermittent sounds a chance to appear. A longer run still cannot guarantee a rare event is captured.

faq.q: Does the weighting change the result?
faq.a: The weighting is a property of the reading you enter. A-weighting follows human hearing, C-weighting keeps more bass, and Z is flat. Use the same one for the reference meter and your offset.

faq.q: Is my audio recorded or uploaded?
faq.a: This calculator only uses the numbers you type. A measurement tool running in your browser analyzes microphone audio locally and does not need to store it.

content_blocks.html: Run a free online echo test and learn in seconds whether your microphone is sending microphone echo, audio feedback or room reverb back into your calls. This online echo detector works in your browser with real-time meters, so there is no download and no sign-up. You only need a microphone and a pair of headphones.

Run a Free Echo Test Online in Your Browser

The echo test takes about a minute. It listens to your voice, shows what the microphone hears as it happens, and flags repeated sound, so echo detection is something you can see rather than guess. Use it before a call or a meeting to hear your setup the way other people do.

Allow Microphone Access

Press the start button and your browser asks for microphone permission. Choose Allow for the input device you want to test. If the prompt never appears, open the site settings for this page and switch the device on. A headset or webcam can be the default input, so pick the right one before you speak.

Speak and Watch Echo Diagnostics

Talk at a normal volume. The oscilloscope draws your waveform live, while the spectrum analyzer splits the sound into bass, midrange and treble. The echo diagnostics panel then scores six things: signal strength, echo loop, feedback risk, reverb tail, signal clarity and noise floor. A clean setup shows a low noise floor and a clarity score that stays high while you speak. Background noise or a noisy fan lowers that score first.

Try Echo Playback With a Delay Slider

Switch on echo playback to hear your voice returned after a delay. Drag the delay slider from 50 ms up to 3 s: short delays sound like a metallic ring, while anything past 100 ms is a clear repeat. Raise the feedback intensity and the repeat loops. The wet mix sets how loud the echo is against the dry signal. Wear headphones for this step, because open speakers turn the playback into real feedback. Make a short recording, then listen to the playback to judge the result.

What a Microphone Test Online Detects

A good microphone test online does more than show a moving bar. It separates three problems that sound alike to the listener: echo, feedback and reverb. Each has a different cause, and each needs a different fix on the speaker, microphone or room side.

What Is Microphone Echo?

Echo happens when your voice is captured, played from another person's speakers, picked up by their microphone and returned to you late. Omnidirectional microphones, such as most laptop mics, collect speaker bleed from every side, so they suffer most. Echo in a meeting is usually a delay of 100 ms or more, long enough to hear the repeat as a separate sound.

Audio Feedback Loop Detection

A feedback loop forms when the microphone hears the speakers and the speakers replay what it hears, round and round, until a squeal or howl appears. The correlation graph in this tool spikes while the loop is still too quiet to hear. Turning off input monitoring in your recording software also matters, because that setting routes the microphone straight to the speakers on purpose.

Room Reverb and Acoustic Reflection

Reverb is the blur left when sound bounces off desks, windows and other hard surfaces and re-enters the microphone a few milliseconds late. Unlike an echo, it does not repeat cleanly; it smears syllables together. The echo correlation graph compares the live signal with a delayed copy of itself using cross-correlation, so reflections show up as bumps while a quiet room stays flat.

Read Your Mic Test Results

After the test, read the device summary before you trust the sound. Any online mic test should list the same fields, and a mic test online that hides them gives you less to work from.

FieldWhat it tells you

Hearing Test: 125 Hz to 20 kHz

The built-in hearing test plays twelve sine wave tones from 125 Hz to 20 kHz, and it backs up the echo results: a tone that sounds doubled or sustained means the room is reflecting sound that can feed an echo, a sign to treat the space before you record. The highest tone you can still hear also marks your hearing range, which for most adults runs to about 18 kHz. The microphone visualizer beside it shows each tone arriving, so you can confirm that both speaker and microphone handle that frequency. A speaker whose frequency response drops off near 16 kHz will look deaf to the top tones, and the frequency range your microphone captures is worth checking the same way.

Works on Every Device and Browser

The test runs in current versions of Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari and Opera on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS. A built-in laptop mic, a USB headset or a podcast microphone all work, and so does a streaming setup, as long as the browser can see the device. Good audio quality starts with a signal the browser can actually read.

Echo Detection at a Home Desk: Timing a Wall Reflection

I'm recording a voice-over tomorrow in a spare room, and I want to know whether the bare wall behind my screen will show up as echo. I run the test with my USB microphone, headphones on, and clap once. The correlation graph shows a small bump right after the clap, while the clarity score stays high, so something is reflecting.

To judge it, I measure the room: the microphone sits 1.9 m from the wall behind it. Sound travels at roughly 343 m/s, and the reflection covers the distance twice, so the delay is t = 2d / c = (2 × 1.9) / 343 ≈ 11.1 ms. That is far below the 50 ms mark where reverb blurs into a distinct repeat, so this is reverb, not echo.

Mic to wallReflection delayWhat you hear
1.9 m11.1 msReverb, a slightly boxy tone
3.4 m19.8 msReverb, a longer tail
17.2 m100 msA clear separate echo

The sensitivity rerun is the useful part: I would need a wall about 17.2 m away for a true 100 ms echo, so no desk setup produces one by reflection alone. If a listener hears a distinct repeat, it comes from the call path, not my room. The number to watch is therefore the clarity score, not the delay. My decision: hang a thick blanket behind the microphone, rerun the test, and aim for a flatter correlation line before I record. One caveat is that this arithmetic only covers the first bounce; a small, hard-walled room adds many reflections, and the simple formula will understate how muddy it sounds.

How to Fix Echo and Feedback After an Echo Detector Check

Once the check points to a cause, fix that cause instead of lowering every setting. In video calls the conferencing app can only cancel what it can predict, so the physical setup comes first.

Use Headphones and Lower Your Speaker Volume

Use headphones first: they separate the speakers from the microphone and remove the feedback path completely. If you must use laptop speakers, lower the speaker volume to 50-70% and move the microphone 30-60 cm away from them. In a group call, mute yourself while others talk.

Enable Acoustic Echo Cancellation in Your App

Zoom, Teams, Google Meet and Discord all include echo cancellation, so turn it on in each app's audio settings and set noise suppression to high where offered. If you also run recording software, disable its input monitoring, and turn off Windows sound effects that add reverb. Then run the echo and feedback detector again. If the echo loop and feedback risk both read clear, the remaining echo is coming from the other side of the call.

Soften the Room With a Directional Microphone

A cardioid pickup pattern hears mostly what sits in front of it, so a directional microphone rejects speaker sound and room reflections that an omnidirectional laptop mic would collect. Add soft furnishings such as rugs, curtains and bookshelves, or hang a thick blanket or acoustic panels behind the microphone to cut the reverb you saw in the diagnostics.

Troubleshooting Your Online Mic Tester

If the waveform stays flat, the mic tester is not receiving a signal. Run a quick mic check of the common causes below before you assume the hardware is broken, because a microphone tester can only report what the browser lets it hear.

Browser Permission, Drivers and Other Apps

Start with browser permission: a blocked site shows no signal at all. Next, close Zoom, Discord or any app that may hold the microphone, confirm the device is enabled in your operating system's privacy settings, update the drivers, and reseat the cable or try another USB port. If another computer picks up the same mic, the hardware is fine and the cause is settings or drivers.

Private by Design: Nothing Leaves Your Device

Every echo analysis on this page runs through the Web Audio API inside your browser, so your voice is processed in memory on your device and never uploaded. It stays private: no account, no stored recording and nothing for a server to keep.

faq.a: Usually another participant is using speakers without echo cancellation, so your voice plays out of their speakers, re-enters their microphone and returns to you late. Ask them to use headphones or enable echo cancellation.

faq.q: What is the difference between echo and reverb?
faq.a: Echo is a distinct repeat that arrives roughly 100 ms or later. Reverb is many short reflections, each under about 50 ms, that blur together as the sound decays.

faq.q: How do I stop audio feedback?
faq.a: Use headphones, lower the speaker volume, move the microphone away from the speakers and mute yourself when you are not talking.

faq.q: Do I need headphones when I use echo playback?
faq.a: Yes. Without headphones, the speakers feed the delayed sound back into the microphone and create real feedback.

content_blocks.html:
The Audio Latency Test measures the round-trip delay between your system playing a sound and your microphone capturing it — your result appears as a latency reading in milliseconds. Plug in headphones to prevent the test tone feeding back through your mic, click Start Test, and the tool plays a short click then times how long your mic takes to detect it. Your latency result tells you how much delay to expect on video calls, live recordings, or any setup where mic-to-output timing matters. Record your latency readings in a free notepad at notepadly.online.

Understanding Audio Latency

Latency Rating Suitable For
<10 ms Excellent Professional music production, live monitoring
10-20 ms Very Good Music production, gaming with audio
20-40 ms Good Video calls, casual gaming, streaming
40-100 ms Acceptable Voice calls, video conferencing
>100 ms High Noticeable delay - may cause echo issues

Reducing Audio Latency

Hardware Tips

  • Use a dedicated audio interface
  • Connect via USB 3.0 or Thunderbolt
  • Avoid Bluetooth for low-latency needs
  • Use wired headphones

Software Tips

  • Use ASIO drivers on Windows
  • Reduce audio buffer size
  • Close unnecessary audio applications
  • Update audio drivers regularly

Having issues? Check our troubleshooting guide for more solutions.

How to Take the Audio Latency Test

  1. Put on headphones — open-air speakers cause acoustic feedback that corrupts the measurement. Wired headphones give the most accurate round-trip latency reading.
  2. Click Allow when the browser asks for microphone access. The test needs your mic to capture the reference tone it plays.
  3. Keep the room quiet — any background noise can interfere with the detection algorithm and inflate the latency reading.
  4. Click Start Test and wait for the progress bar to complete. The tool plays a short tone, listens for it through your microphone, and calculates the round-trip delay.
  5. Run the test three to five times and use the average reading — individual results can vary slightly due to browser scheduling.
  6. Compare your result to the latency rating table: under 20ms is excellent for music and calls; above 100ms indicates a problem worth addressing.

What Is Audio Latency? Understanding Sound Delay in Your System

Audio latency is the total time between a sound event (a key pressed, a voice spoken, a signal triggered) and when it is audible through speakers or headphones. Every device in your signal chain adds a small delay: the driver, the audio engine, the digital-to-analogue converter, and the amplifier all contribute. The sum of all these delays is your system's total audio latency, measured in milliseconds. Check your full audible range with a hearing test online — from 20Hz bass to 20kHz treble.

Base Latency vs Output Latency vs Round-Trip Latency

Base latency is the minimum processing delay of the audio engine — the time from when software sends a signal to when the hardware begins outputting it. Output latency is the delay introduced by the output device's buffer. Round-trip latency is what this test measures: the full loop from output to microphone capture — which includes both output and input delays simultaneously. For real-time recording and live monitoring, round-trip latency is the most relevant measurement.

Browser Audio Latency vs DAW Input Latency

Browser-based audio latency tests give a useful estimate but cannot match the precision of dedicated DAW buffer analysis. Browsers add an inherent processing overhead — typically 20–40ms even on fast hardware — because the Web Audio API runs through a non-realtime scheduler. A DAW using ASIO drivers on Windows or Core Audio on macOS bypasses this overhead and can achieve sub-5ms round-trip latency. Use this online audio latency test to diagnose general system performance; use your DAW's built-in latency report for music production calibration.

Audio Latency by Use Case — What Is an Acceptable Sound Delay?

The right latency threshold depends entirely on what you are doing with the audio. A video call tolerates delays that would be completely unacceptable in a live recording session.

Music Production and Live Monitoring: Minimum Input Latency Required

When recording instruments or vocals, musicians monitor their own performance through headphones in real time. Any latency above 10ms is perceivable as a slight "doubling" effect — the direct sound from the instrument arrives slightly before the monitored sound through the headphones. Professional recordings target under 5ms total round-trip latency. If your audio latency test returns 10–20ms, it is workable for most home recording; above 30ms, you will notice the delay while singing or playing.

Gaming and Live Streaming — Audio Delay and Sync Issues

Gaming audio latency above 100ms makes it difficult to use audio cues to react to in-game events (gunshots, footsteps). For streamers, audio delay causes the voice commentary to fall out of sync with on-screen action. Most streaming software lets you add a video delay offset to compensate, but reducing the underlying audio latency in the first place is always preferable. A result of 20–50ms is acceptable for casual gaming; competitive play benefits from anything below 20ms.

Video Calls and Online Meetings

Conference call software (Zoom, Teams, Meet) buffers and resamples audio, adding 40–150ms of its own delay on top of your system latency. For this use case, your microphone latency reading from this test is less critical — the app's own processing dominates. That said, a high system latency above 100ms can compound the app's delay and make you sound consistently late in conversations. Under 50ms system latency is ideal for smooth call audio.

How to Reduce Audio Latency and Minimise Sound Delay

ASIO Drivers for Low-Latency Audio on Windows

ASIO (Audio Stream Input/Output) is a driver protocol developed by Steinberg that bypasses Windows' standard audio engine, dramatically cutting latency. If you use a USB audio interface, install its ASIO driver from the manufacturer's website. If no dedicated driver is available, ASIO4ALL is a free wrapper that gives most Windows machines access to low-latency ASIO routing. Most DAWs let you switch between WASAPI and ASIO — always choose ASIO for recording work. On macOS, Core Audio already provides near-ASIO performance natively. The online mic recorder captures audio from your microphone with no upload and no account required.

Reducing Buffer Size to Lower Microphone Latency

The audio buffer is a short memory queue that holds samples before they are processed. A smaller buffer reduces latency but increases CPU load — if the CPU cannot fill the buffer in time, you get audio dropouts and glitches. For recording, set the buffer to 64–256 samples. For mixing or playback only, 512–1024 samples is fine. If you get crackling at low buffer sizes, close all background applications and check that no other software is claiming exclusive audio access to your device.

Wired vs Bluetooth: Which Has Lower Audio Delay?

Bluetooth audio introduces 100–300ms of codec-dependent latency. Aptx Low Latency (aptX LL) reduces this to 40ms; Bluetooth LE Audio (LC3) targets 20–30ms. Even the best Bluetooth codecs cannot match a wired USB or 3.5 mm connection, which typically adds under 5ms at the hardware level. If your audio latency test returns values above 100ms and you are on Bluetooth, switching to a wired connection is the single most effective change you can make.

faq_heading: Audio Latency Test — Frequently Asked Questions

faq.q: What causes high audio latency in a browser?
faq.a: Browsers process audio through the Web Audio API, which runs on a non-realtime scheduler. This adds inherent overhead of 20–40ms regardless of your hardware. Additional causes include: a large audio buffer set in your OS driver settings, background applications competing for CPU, Bluetooth audio routing, or an outdated audio driver. For the browser-based audio latency test to show a low reading, all these factors need to be minimised simultaneously.

faq.q: Why does Bluetooth always show high audio latency?
faq.a: Bluetooth audio uses lossy compression codecs (SBC, AAC, aptX) that add encoding and decoding time. The Bluetooth radio protocol also adds packet transmission delay. Even with modern low-latency codecs, you should expect 40–200ms of additional delay versus a wired connection. Some earbuds in "gaming mode" switch to a lower-latency codec specifically to reduce this — check if your device has this option in its companion app.

faq.q: Is the audio latency test the same as a network ping test?
faq.a: No — they measure completely different things. A network ping test measures how long a data packet takes to travel across a network. This audio latency test measures how long it takes for your device to produce a sound and for that sound to be captured by your microphone — entirely local, no network involved. Poor network ping does not directly cause audio latency within your computer's sound system.

faq.q: My latency reading is 5ms but audio still feels delayed — why?
faq.a: Browser-based tests estimate latency using AudioContext.baseLatency and AudioContext.outputLatency — values reported by the browser, not directly measured. The browser may report a low hardware latency while adding its own scheduling delay on top. Additionally, if you are experiencing perceived audio delay in a specific application (video call, DAW, game), that application may be adding its own buffering that this test does not account for. Test within the specific application's own latency settings.

faq.q: What is ASIO and does it reduce audio latency significantly?
faq.a: ASIO bypasses the Windows Kernel Mixer, which adds up to 30ms of extra latency. With a quality audio interface and ASIO driver, total round-trip latency of 3–6ms is achievable on modern hardware. Without ASIO (using WASAPI or DirectSound), typical Windows latency is 20–50ms. The improvement is significant for music production. ASIO has no equivalent in browser audio — this is why browser-based tests always show higher latency than DAW measurements.

faq.q: Can I use this test to calibrate latency for my DAW recording setup?
faq.a: Use it as a starting point for diagnosing whether your audio interface is performing as expected. For precise DAW calibration, use your DAW's built-in round-trip latency measurement or a dedicated hardware latency tester. The online mic recorder is also useful for checking whether your recorded audio drifts out of sync over time, which indicates a clock rate mismatch rather than a latency issue.
