content_blocks.html: When you ask a computer to show my speakers, you really want two answers: which of the types of speakers you own, and whether each one still plays sound. This guide lets you test your setup first, then explains how every loudspeaker turns an audio signal into the music you hear.

Show My Speakers: Test the Speakers You Already Have

Not sure your speakers are connected and working? A quick sound test answers that in under a minute, right in the browser. Your computer sends an audio signal to a playback device, and the operating system decides which playback device receives it, so the first job is confirming that the right one is selected. A laptop might quietly send sound to a monitor, a pair of Bluetooth headphones or the built-in speaker instead of the pair on your desk. Check this before you blame your whole home audio setup, or assume the audio system itself is broken.

Run a sound test on each speaker channel

Play a short tone through the left speaker, then through the right speaker. If the tone arrives from the correct side each time, your stereo speakers are wired the right way round and the left channel and right channel are both alive. Turn the volume all the way up for this check only, because a speaker that sounds dead may simply be playing very quietly. Then bring the volume back down before you play music. Your hearing varies from day to day, so repeat the check once before you decide a speaker is faulty.

What to do if your speakers give no sound

Work through the cheap fixes first, since most failures are loose cables rather than broken hardware:

  • Make sure the speakers are powered on and plugged into electricity.
  • Check that the speaker cable runs to the green jack on the back of a desktop, or to the headphone socket on a laptop.
  • Look at the volume in your operating system and on any physical knob.
  • Confirm that the correct playback device is enabled, because the system may be sending the tone to a different jack.

If nothing helps, the audio driver may be at fault. Search for the latest audio driver for your sound card from its maker, install it, restart and run the test again. A missing or outdated audio driver is the most common reason a healthy speaker system stays silent after an update.

Fix stereo speakers that only play one channel

When only one side makes noise, the two speakers are often not connected to each other. In many desktop designs a single wire runs from the computer to the main unit, and you must link the second speaker to the first yourself. Swap the left and right plugs to find out whether the cable or the speaker is the problem, because the dead side follows the faulty part.

Types of Speakers You Can Have at Home

Every home has its own mix of home speakers, and each type of speakers is built for a particular job: some favour music, some favour movies, and some favour the garden. Knowing the main types of speakers helps you recognise what you already own and decide which one to add next. The table sums up the usual fit for each, so choose by the sound you want, not by the badge.

Speaker typeBest forWhere it sits
Floor-standingFull-range music and moviesOn the floor, away from walls
BookshelfSmall rooms and desksShelf, stand or table
In-wall / in-ceilingHidden surround soundBuilt into the wall or ceiling
SoundbarClearer TV dialogueUnder or above the TV
SubwooferDeep bassFloor, near a wall or corner
OutdoorPatios and gardensWeatherproof mount

Floor-Standing Speakers

Floor-standing speakers, also called tower speakers, are tall cabinets that hold several drivers and a large enclosure, often called the speaker cabinet. They reproduce deep bass and clear vocals with little help, which makes them a favourite when you want a complete sound system for a living room.

Bookshelf Speakers

Bookshelf speakers are compact two-way designs that fit on a shelf, a desk or a stand. They suit smaller rooms and give detailed sound without eating floor space, and many listeners count them among the best speakers for a first stereo pair.

In-Wall and In-Ceiling Speakers

In-wall speakers and in-ceiling speakers disappear into the room, so the only thing you notice is the sound. They are popular for home cinema because they create surround sound without cabinets on the floor, and an angled tweeter helps aim the sound at the seats. Aesthetics are the main reason people choose them.

Soundbars for TV Sound

A soundbar is a long, slim cabinet with several drivers that sits under or above your TV. It packs the left, centre and right speakers into one box, so dialogue is easy to follow and setup takes minutes. Soundbars are a smart pick when the room is too tight for separate speakers.

Subwoofers for Deep Bass

A subwoofer handles only the lowest notes, the rumble in an action film or the kick drum in a dance track. Because low bass is hard to locate by ear, a single subwoofer can sit in a corner and still feel natural. Most good speaker systems pair one subwoofer with smaller speakers, and some larger rooms use two subwoofers to even out the bass.

Outdoor Speakers

Outdoor speakers are sealed against rain, sun and wind, so you can play music at a barbecue or in the garden without worry. They trade a little sound quality for durability, and they often need a mount rather than a stand.

Surround Speakers

Surround speakers sit beside or behind the listening position and create the sense of being inside the scene, which matters for a home theater and for games. They are the last speakers most people add to a home cinema, after the front three.

Wireless vs. Wired Speakers and Active vs. Passive Speaker Systems

Two choices shape every purchase: how audio reaches the speaker, and where the amplifier lives. Wireless models stream over Bluetooth or Wi-Fi and keep a room tidy, while wired speakers use a cable and usually offer steadier, higher-quality sound. A cable never drops out, which is why many hi-fi owners stay wired for their main system.

Active Speakers

Active speakers have a built-in amplifier, so you connect a source straight to them. They are simple, compact and ideal for a desk or a small apartment, and they save you from matching an external receiver.

Passive Speakers

Passive speakers contain no amplifier. They need an external amplifier or receiver, which gives you freedom to upgrade each part separately and to chase high fidelity over time. The trade-off is a little more wiring and a little more planning.

Wireless Speakers

Wireless speakers still need power, and most also carry a built-in amplifier, so a wireless speaker is usually an active design with a radio inside. A premium wireless loudspeaker can match a wired pair for sound, but its batteries and network connection add things that can fail.

Checking a Bookshelf Speaker System Against a 45-Watt Amplifier

I'm helping a friend work out whether the speakers she already has, a bookshelf pair on her desk shelf, can fill a room properly, or whether she needs a bigger amplifier. The decision: keep the 45-watt amplifier she owns, or spend money on a stronger one. The spec sheet gives 87.5 dB sensitivity at 1 W and 1 m, 8 ohms, and her chair sits 2.6 m from each loudspeaker.

I run the speaker specifications through the level formula in this order: start with sensitivity, add 10 log10(45) = 16.5 dB for the power, then subtract 20 log10(2.6) = 8.3 dB for distance. That gives 87.5 + 16.5 − 8.3 = 95.7 dB peak from one speaker. A recomputation by hand with a calculator agrees to 0.1 dB.

The reference point is 85 dB, the average level most film mixers calibrate to, with peaks well above it. Reaching 85 dB on average needs only 3.8 W, so everyday listening is easy. The trouble is headroom: 95.7 dB leaves just 10.7 dB above that average, and loud passages in a film or a dense mix can need 15 dB, which is about 120 W at this distance.

What stands out is that distance is the cheapest upgrade: moving her chair closer buys 2.3 dB, as much as a 70 percent bigger amplifier. The input to watch is sensitivity, because a 3.5 dB gap needs more than double the power to close. One caveat: a rating quoted at 2.83 V rather than 1 W reads roughly 3 dB higher on a 4-ohm speaker, so check the fine print before comparing two sheets. My call is to keep the amplifier and move the chair, then revisit the speaker system only if clipping appears at her normal volume.

Inside a Loudspeaker: How Speaker Drivers Make Sound

A loudspeaker, often just called a speaker, combines one or more drivers, an enclosure and the electrical connections, sometimes with a crossover network. The driver is an electroacoustic part that converts an electrical audio signal into sound waves by moving air. The dynamic loudspeaker was invented in 1925 by Edward Kellogg and Chester Rice, and almost every loudspeaker made today still follows their moving-coil idea. Each of these speaker drivers has a job tied to a range of pitch, and a driver reproduces a band of frequencies best when its size matches the wavelength it must move.

That relationship is simple: λ = c / f where c is the speed of sound, about 343 m/s in air, and f is the frequency. A 20 Hz bass note stretches about 17 m, while a 10 kHz note is only 3.4 cm, which is why one cone cannot do everything well.

Think of a three-way loudspeaker as a team. The drivers share the audio, each driver stays inside its comfort zone, and the sound that reaches you is the sum of every driver working together. A single driver pushed beyond its range adds distortion, so a well-designed loudspeaker keeps each driver away from notes it cannot reproduce cleanly. Larger drivers move more air for bass, smaller drivers react faster for treble, and the match between drivers decides how natural the sound feels in your room. When you compare speaker systems, count the drivers and check how the maker divides the work between them, because more drivers do not always mean better sound.

Voice Coil, Diaphragm and Magnet

When the audio signal passes through the voice coil, a coil of wire sitting in the field of a permanent magnet, the coil moves back and forth. The coil is attached to the diaphragm, usually shaped as a speaker cone for strength, and the diaphragm pushes the air to make sound waves. A suspension keeps the voice coil centred, and a basket holds the whole assembly rigid. Because a loudspeaker works like a microphone in reverse, the same moving-coil design can serve in both.

Full-Range Drivers and Component Speakers

A full-range driver tries to cover the whole audible band with a single diaphragm. A full-range design is cheap, simple and phase-coherent, but a single cone struggles at the extremes. Component speakers split the job: the woofers and tweeters are separate and each is tuned for its own range, which usually sounds fuller. Many car doors use a full-range pair, while an upgrade often means moving to component speakers.

Woofer, Mid-Range Driver and Tweeter

A woofer is the large driver for low frequencies, and a subwoofer goes lower still. A mid-range driver covers the voice region, and the tweeter is the small, light driver for the highest notes. In a two-way loudspeaker one woofer and one tweeter share the work, while a three-way loudspeaker adds a mid-range driver. A coaxial design places the tweeter in the centre of the woofer to save space. Treble from the tweeters sets how airy a recording feels, and the woofers deliver most of the bass.

Crossover Networks and Enclosures

The crossover inside each loudspeaker is a filter that sends each driver only the frequencies it handles well, so the tweeter never receives heavy bass. The enclosure matters just as much: without a cabinet, sound from the rear of the cone cancels the sound from the front. A sealed enclosure gives tight bass, while a bass reflex design adds a tuned port that extends it. A solid enclosure also stops panels from rattling and keeps the loudspeaker free of distortion.

Speaker Wiring Connections

Most passive models use binding posts that accept bare speaker wire or banana plugs. Use a gauge of speaker cable thick enough for the run, and keep both loudspeaker leads the same length so the left speaker and right speaker see the same resistance.

Reading Your Speakers' Specifications

The numbers on a speaker box look intimidating, but three of them predict most of what you will hear. They tell you how loud a loudspeaker plays, how much it needs from your amplifier and whether the pair will produce balanced sound in your room. Start with sensitivity, because it sets how hard your amplifier must work.

Sensitivity and Efficiency

Sensitivity states how loud a driver plays at one metre with one watt, measured in decibels. A higher figure means the speaker plays louder from the same power, so a 92 dB model needs far less amplifier effort than an 84 dB model. Efficiency is the same idea as a percentage, and the two are related but not identical. Because decibels use logarithms, the change between two power levels follows Δ L = 10log₁₀(P_2 / P_1) so doubling a 50-watt amplifier to 100 watts adds only 3 dB.

Impedance and Electrical Characteristics

Impedance, measured in ohms, is the load the loudspeaker presents to the amplifier. Most home models are rated at 8 ohms, and some at 4 ohms, which asks the amplifier for more current. Impedance rises and falls across the frequency range, so a nominal rating is only a guide. Match it to your amplifier or receiver and the electrical side takes care of itself.

Power Handling in Watts

Power handling is how much power a speaker takes before the voice coil overheats or the cone is damaged, rated in watts. Pick speakers whose rating sits above your amplifier output and you avoid the most common cause of burnt drivers, which is clipping from an underpowered amplifier played too loud and distorting the sound.

Choosing the Right Speakers for Your Space

The right speakers are the ones that suit your room, your budget and what you play. A beautiful pair in the wrong space still sounds poor, so think about the room before the brand.

Room Size and Speaker Placement

Room size sets how much bass you can use: a big space needs more output, while a small one pushes bookshelf pairs toward the wall and makes bass boomy. Placement matters too. Corners boost bass response, which can turn a small room muddy. Keep each speaker away from corners, aim the tweeters at ear height and form a rough triangle with your seat to hold a steady soundstage across the whole speaker system. When the listening environment is lively, soft furnishings tame reflections.

What Will You Use Them For?

Music lovers should look for balanced, detailed bookshelf or tower speakers. Movie fans should start from the center channel, because it carries most of the dialogue and a large share of the soundtrack. Pick front speakers that match its tone for timbre matching, so panning across the front sounds smooth, and use surround speakers that are close in tone. Good imaging depends on that match more than on price.

Car Speakers and Factory Speaker Upgrades

For car speakers, first check what fits your vehicle, since door and dash openings dictate the speaker size. A voice-matched set from the same brand and series keeps front and rear consistent. Replacing the factory speakers is among the cheapest ways to improve car audio, and rear speakers matter less if you rarely carry passengers. If the budget is tight, upgrade the front pair first, then buy new speakers for the rear later.

faq.q: Why can't I see all my connected speakers in the list?
faq.a: Browser audio device enumeration requires microphone permission — the browser uses mic permission as a gate to prevent fingerprinting via device enumeration. If you denied microphone access previously, the device list may be incomplete or show only the default output. Grant microphone access when prompted (even if you have no microphone) and refresh the page. Also, some audio devices register only as input devices and will not appear in the speaker output list.

faq.q: What does "Default Device" mean in my speaker details?
faq.a: The default device is the audio output endpoint that applications use unless they specify a different one. When you play a YouTube video or join a Zoom call without selecting a specific output, the audio goes to the default device. You can change the default in OS sound settings (Windows: Sound Control Panel → Playback tab; macOS: System Settings → Sound → Output). The speaker detail table shows whether a device is currently set as your default.

faq.q: Why does my speaker show as "disconnected" even though I can hear audio?
faq.a: Some browsers cannot always determine the live connection status of audio endpoints, particularly for HDMI outputs and Bluetooth devices. The status shown is reported by the OS driver, which may lag behind the actual hardware state. If audio is playing through the device, it is functionally connected regardless of what the status label says. Use the built-in speaker test in this tool to confirm audio output rather than relying solely on the status indicator.

faq.q: Can I see the model name and specifications of my speakers through the browser?
faq.a: The browser can only access what the OS audio driver exposes — typically the device name, device ID, group ID, sample rate, and channel count. Detailed hardware specifications like driver size, power rating, or frequency response are not available through any browser API. For full hardware details on a specific speaker model, check the manufacturer's product page using the model name shown in the device list.

This free tone generator plays a pure tone in your browser, so you can set a frequency in Hz and hear that audio signal at once. Use it to check your hearing, tune a string or test a speaker, and keep the tones short while you do.

How to Use This Online Tone Generator

  • Press play and start at a low volume.
  • Move the slider to your frequency.
  • Wear headphones, or place speakers at ear height.
  • Choose a waveform, then press stop when you finish.

Set the Frequency with the Slider

Drag the slider anywhere from 1 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Fine-grained steps let you land on 1,000 Hz, a common reference level, or on 20 Hz, where deep bass fades out. To move an octave, halve or double the value: 440 Hz becomes 220 Hz or 880 Hz.

Pick a Sine Wave, Square Wave, Sawtooth or Triangle

The pure shape is the cleanest waveform. A square wave, sawtooth or triangle adds overtones that change the sound character. The real-time visualization draws each waveform on an oscilloscope, and the 44.1kHz sample rate keeps it smooth.

Frequency Generator Features and Common Hz Values

Under the hood, this tone generator runs on the Web Audio API and acts as a sine wave generator by default. Use stereo balance to pan a tone, switch to mono, run a sweep, or layer binaural beats and mixed tones from several tabs. Finding a 37 Hz Room Mode with a Sine Wave Generator

My desk speakers sound boomy on one bass note and thin on the next, and I want to know whether the room is to blame. The room is 4.62 m long, so I work out where its first lengthwise resonance should fall before touching the slider: speed of sound divided by twice the length. At 20 °C sound travels at about 343.4 m/s, so 343.4 ÷ (2 × 4.62) gives 37.17 Hz, with repeats at 74.33 Hz and 111.50 Hz.

Then I open the sine wave generator, pick the sine wave so no overtones muddy the test, and set the volume low. I step the frequency through 30, 34, 37, 40 and 45 Hz while sitting in my usual chair. The loudest swell lands at 37 Hz, and a second bump at 74 Hz confirms the pattern. What stands out is that the chair sits 2.31 m from the back wall, exactly half the room length, where a first mode is strongest.

The sensitivity rerun is short: a hot afternoon moves the mode about 0.5 Hz, so I repeat the 37 Hz step in the generator at 38 Hz as well. Against the 20 Hz lower edge of human hearing, 37 Hz is comfortably audible, so this is a real problem, not a curiosity.

My next step is concrete: slide the chair 40 cm toward the back wall, then re-run the sweep at 30, 34, 37, 40 and 45 Hz and compare the swell. One caveat keeps me honest: if the dip stays put when I move the speaker, the driver's own roll-off may be the cause, and laptop speakers cannot play 37 Hz at all. The number to watch is the first mode, because it carries the most energy.

What a Sound Generator Is Used For

In classrooms, students run science experiments with it, and audio engineers rely on it for equipment testing and research.

Hearing Test and Tinnitus Matching

A hearing test starts mid-range and works outward to find the top of your hearing range. To match a tinnitus pitch with it, try 7,350 Hz, then check 3,675 Hz and 14,700 Hz, one octave away. The generator can play solfeggio or masking tones at a chosen Hz for sound therapy, meditation, relaxation, focus or sleep routines, but this is not a medical device.

Tuning Instruments and Ear Training

Musicians know music tuning needs a steady reference: play 440 Hz and match your string. Ear training uses test tones to learn intervals, while harmonics show why an octave sounds so consistent.

Speaker, Subwoofer and Audio Equipment Testing

Sweep a subwoofer through sub-bass to find rattles, then climb to treble to check the tweeters. A sudden loud spot reveals a resonant frequency, a sign of resonance in the cabinet or room. Calibrating amplifiers and mixers, audio level alignment for radio, acoustics and equalization all rely on a steady signal, and calibration against a known level beats guessing.

Hz Generator Safety and Volume Limits

A hz generator can damage speakers and your ears at extreme levels, even with quiet tones, so safety comes first. Set a comfortable level on a mid-range tone and never go above it. The same caution applies to square and sawtooth waves, and to white noise or pink noise in desktop software. Lower the volume before you change frequency or waveform.

Hertz Generator in a Browser or as a Download

The online sound generator works in Chrome, Firefox and Safari on a desktop, tablet or mobile, using your device's audio output with no install.

Tone Generator Software Requirements

Offline tone generator software suits long desktop sessions, within your sound card's limits. Typical packages bundle a sound frequency generator, a white noise generator and a tone and sound generator toolbar that saves files, and a frequency tone generator app on a phone gives the same output. The browser version needs only a current browser, an audio output and a volume control.

faq.q: What frequency range can an online tone generator play?
faq.a: Most browser tone generators cover roughly 1 Hz to 20,000 Hz, which spans human hearing from deep sub-bass to the highest treble. How low you actually hear depends on your speakers or headphones, since small drivers cannot reproduce very low tones.

faq.q: Is it safe to play high or low frequencies?
faq.a: Extreme frequencies at high volume can damage your hearing and your speakers. Find a comfortable level on a mid-range tone, such as 1,000 Hz, and do not go far above it, even when you cannot hear much.

faq.q: What are the different waveforms for?
faq.a: A sine wave is a pure tone with no overtones and suits hearing and tuning tests. Square, sawtooth and triangle waves add overtones, giving a buzzier or brighter sound that is useful for checking speaker response.

faq.q: Can I use a tone generator to tune an instrument?
faq.a: Yes. Play a reference such as 440 Hz and match your string or pipe to it by ear. The Nearest Note result shows which note a frequency is closest to and how many cents sharp or flat it is.

faq.q: How do I find my tinnitus frequency?
faq.a: Move the frequency until a tone seems to match the ringing, then check one octave higher and one octave lower, because tones an octave apart are easy to confuse. This is not a medical device, so see a clinician for diagnosis.

faq.q: How do I share a specific tone with someone?
faq.a: Copy the Shareable Link Settings result and add it to the page address. It stores your frequency, waveform, volume and balance, so the other person opens the same tone.

faq.q: Does a tone generator work offline?
faq.a: Browser tools need the page loaded first. For fully offline use, install desktop tone generator software, which can also save a tone as a WAV file.

content_blocks.html: Run this stereo test to hear whether your left speaker and right speaker each play on the correct side, straight from your browser. Press Left, Center or Right and listen: the audio should follow the side you picked. In about a minute you will know whether your speakers, headphones or earbuds have reversed, silent or merged channels, and what to fix next.

How to run a left and right audio test on your speakers

Sit where you normally listen, face the speakers and follow these steps. This test doubles as a left and right speaker test for any laptop, phone or desktop audio setup.

  1. Start low. Set the volume on your computer, output device or amplifier to a comfortable level, because test sounds can be harsher than music.
  2. Press Left. The sound should come only from the left speaker or the left headphone cup.
  3. Press Right. The same sound should move entirely to the right side.
  4. Press Center. With matching speakers, the sound should sit in the middle, not lean left or right.
  5. Use the pan sweep. The signal should glide smoothly from left to right with no jumps.

Keep the playback level steady between presses, so a difference you hear comes from the output and not from a louder tone.

Stereo sound test results: phase, polarity and balance

Match what you heard to the table below. Every row points to a different cause, so change one thing at a time.

What you hearWhat it meansCheck next
Left plays left, Right plays rightChannel mapping is correctNothing; test your app's own output
Left plays rightChannels are reversedSpeaker cables and mixer mapping
One side is silentOne output path is missingBalance, connector, known-good cable
Both sides play togetherStereo is summed to monoAccessibility and Bluetooth settings
Center sounds hollowSpeakers may be out of phasePolarity of one speaker's wires

This stereo sound test checks which side each signal reaches. It cannot prove polarity, but a centered voice that sounds thin suggests speakers pushing against each other. When both speakers are in phase, the center image is solid and bass is full; out of phase, it turns hollow. If only a single channel seems off, the sound itself is fine and the fault sits in the chain.

Fixing left/right stereo wiring that plays reversed

If Left plays right, first confirm you are facing the speakers. Then trace the cable from each output to its speaker: the left output must reach the left amplifier input. On an RCA cable, red is right and white is left, so check both ends of the connector. Bypass any virtual routing layer and compare a trusted recording in another player. If it plays wrong there too, correct the mapping you found, and never rewire powered hardware while it is live. A wired set-up with long speaker cables is the usual culprit; swapped plugs are the second, and a right channel on the left almost always traces to one of them. Wireless pairs rarely swap, so a reversed result there suggests a software setting.

Silent speaker or earbud: a quick stereo check

When one side makes no sound, open your system settings and make sure the balance is centered. Reseat the connector, remove adapters, and repeat this stereo check through a known-good output. That comparison shows whether the output path or the drivers inside one speaker have failed, because a fault that follows the device is not your output. For wiring you can reach safely, swap the two source cables once and replay Center: if the silence moves, suspect the source output.

Headphone test for earbuds and headsets

This headphone test uses the same buttons. If one earbud is quiet, clean its mesh, then wear the headphones the other way around. If the weak side follows the earbud, the unit is at fault. A headset on a phone can also fail when Bluetooth switches to call mode.

When stereo channels collapse to mono

If pressing Left plays through both sides, the route may be summing to mono. Look at your mono audio accessibility setting, a Bluetooth call profile, a single-speaker phone and any mixer between the browser and the speakers. Windows, macOS and iPhone each hide the switch under accessibility. Press Center to separate mono from a headset fault: with mono, Center still sounds normal, but a headset plug that misses its ground contact makes Center nearly vanish. Playing through both sides can also fool your hearing at low volume, so repeat it louder only if it is comfortable.

Stereo balance check when one side is quieter

A quieter side that still plays points to level, not routing. Move the balance slider to the middle, then swap earbuds or headphones around. Your hearing may differ between ears, and this audio test cannot tell that from the equipment.

How a browser stereo test routes the signal

The page builds a tone with the Web Audio API and passes it through a stereo panner running from -1 (full left) to +1 (full right). An equal-power pan keeps loudness steady while the signal moves:

g_L = cos(((p+1)π) / 4), g_R = sin(((p+1)π) / 4)

At Center (p = 0) both outputs carry about 0.707 of full level, at p = -0.5 the gains are 0.924 and 0.383. Your browser may block playback until you click, so press a button first.

Pink noise or a sine wave tone

A sine wave makes channel identity clear. Pink noise spreads energy across a wider band, so a level difference between sides is easier to notice. Neither is a calibrated measurement, and background noise in your room will still affect what you hear.

Stereo test with no microphone and no upload

The signal is generated locally. This page never asks for a microphone and never uploads your sound anywhere.

A leaning center image, traced with a left and right audio test

The decision on my desk is simple: do I buy new cables, or just move the chair? My bookshelf speakers sit 1.20 m apart and my chair is close to the tip of that triangle. I press Left, then Right, then Center, at a low level each time. Left plays left and Right plays right, so the wiring is fine. Yet Center clearly sits left of my monitor. The channel test has already ruled out reversed or missing sides, which leaves geometry and level.

I measure the distances with a tape: 1.20 m to the right speaker, 0.89 m to the left. That 0.31 m gap delays the right speaker by 0.90 ms (0.31 m ÷ 343 m/s = 0.0009 s). Sound that arrives first pulls the image toward its speaker, the precedence effect, so Center leans left even though both channels carry the same level.

My first instinct is the balance control, replaying the middle press after each change to see whether the image recentres. Shifting it toward the right turns the left channel down like this:

At 22% the image recentres, but the left side is now 2.16 dB quieter, and a level gap of around 1 dB is often cited as audible on steady tones. That is a trade-off I do not want, so I reset balance to the middle. The number to watch here is the 0.31 m distance difference, not the decibels, because it fixes the cause rather than hiding it.

I slide the chair 0.31 m to the right and replay Center. The tone now sits between the speakers. The middle press exposed the lean, and the test's real job was ruling out a channel mix-up first. One caution: it only checks routing, so a pass says nothing about distance, and a balance slider cannot correct timing at all. If Center still drifts after the chairs are equal, I would compare a trusted stereo recording next, then check the room.

What this channel test cannot tell you about bass or frequency response

This is a routing check, not a measurement. It does not test frequency response, so it cannot show where a subwoofer rolls off or where small speakers lose bass. Deep bass and sub-bass need a separate frequency sweep, and a low-frequency buzz points to cabinet rattle rather than wiring. Check a subwoofer on its own, since its level and crossover sit outside this test. It also misses distortion and dynamic range limits, and it is not a hearing test or a calibration of your level. Surround sound speakers need their own channel checks, and good stereo separation depends on more than a pass here. Use a dedicated sweep to diagnose range, and keep troubleshooting one change at a time.

Speaker test placement for sharper stereo imaging

Passing the routing check is only the start. Place your loudspeakers an equal distance from your listening position, with the tweeters at ear height and angled inward, so stereophonic sound forms a clear soundstage and the audio feels anchored. Alan Blumlein showed in 1931 that two channels could imitate direction, which is why a centered image should land midway between the pair. Keep the speakers away from walls, since the room adds acoustic boom, and re-run the test after moving anything in a home theater setup.

Stereo audio test passes but the file is wrong

If this sound test routes correctly yet an exported WAV has a missing or swapped channel, inspect the file rather than your speakers. A known-good recording in another player settles the question, and troubleshooting the source file first saves swapping cables for nothing.

faq.q: How do I know if my speakers are wired correctly?

faq.q: Why does the left channel play through both sides?

Free Online Bass Test: How to Run It

Drag the slider or type a number, press play, and press stop when you are done. The tone generator behind this bass generator outputs one clean test tone at a time, and the sweep descends from 150 Hz toward 10 Hz so you hear exactly where it vanishes, while a voiceover names each step in hertz and the visualization toggle draws the sine tone. It works in any browser, on a laptop or smartphone, through any output device. Begin at a low volume, because this bass tester is meant for careful listening to clean sound.

Sub-Bass vs Mid-Bass in a Low Frequency Range Test

A low frequency range test spans about 10Hz to 200Hz, in two halves. Sub-bass (20 Hz to 60 Hz) is the rumble you feel in movie theaters and clubs; the tactile vibration matters more than what you hear. Mid-bass (60 Hz to 200 Hz) carries the punch and warmth of kick drums and a bass guitar. Anywhere in the low frequency range, the human hearing range sets the floor at 20 Hz.

Bass Response of Subwoofers, Speakers and Headphones

Reproducing the lowest frequency means moving air. A subwoofer with large drivers in a sealed enclosure holds 30Hz cleanly, laptop speakers roll off near 80Hz, and budget earbuds stop around 40Hz. Premium headphones and over-ear headphones reach 20 Hz because the sealed ear canal acts as a pressure chamber that lifts the low-end by 12 dB per octave. Repeat the bass test on each audio device and compare its frequency response by noting where the tone disappears.

Wavelength Formula for Your Lowest Frequency

Say the sweep first becomes audible at 34 Hz on your speakers: λ = c / f = 343 / 34 ≈ 10.1 m A wave that long needs big drivers, which is why small ones fade first.

Using the Bass Tester on Two Pairs of Headphones

Priya is choosing which headphones to take on a long flight: her over-ear pair or her earbuds. She wants whichever plays deeper, so she runs the sweep on each, in a quiet room, at the same volume, and writes down the number the voiceover reads when the rising tone first becomes audible.

The over-ear pair gives 27.4 Hz; the earbuds give 41.0 Hz. Dividing the speed of sound by each frequency gives the wavelengths: 343 ÷ 27.4 = 12.5 m and 343 ÷ 41.0 = 8.4 m. Against the common benchmark that headphones hearing 30 Hz or lower without distortion have excellent bass, the over-ear pair clears the bar and the earbuds do not.

She then reruns the over-ear test with one cushion lifted a few millimetres. The first audible tone jumps to 52.0 Hz, nearly an octave higher, because a leak breaks the sealed ear canal chamber that gives headphones their low-end lift. That is the edge case worth knowing: a single result is only valid for the fit you tested, so a loose cushion or glasses frame can make good headphones look weak.

My read is that the seal matters more than the model here. The number to watch is the sealed result, and she decides to keep the over-ear pair, re-seat the cushions over her glasses before the flight, and rerun the sweep once more; if it still reads above 30 Hz, she will pack the earbuds as backup.

Spot Harmonic Distortion With a Sine Wave

During the test, tones below 20 Hz should stay inaudible. If you hear something at 15 Hz, your speaker or subwoofer is adding distortion rather than playing the signal. Rattling means loose parts, and a sudden volume drop shows roll off. A sine wave keeps the waveform clean, so any harmonic distortion you hear is the gear's own, and the transient response stays easy to judge when you are tuning. Judge performance and quality by how undistorted the output stays.

Room Acoustics and Low-Frequency Tones

If the tone drops out or swells at certain spots, your room, not your gear, is often the cause: standing waves create dead spots and boom.

Speaker Placement and the Subwoofer Crawl

Put a woofer in a corner so the walls reinforce it, or try the subwoofer crawl: place it at your seat and crawl around to find the smoothest spot. Rerun the test at each position and keep the one where the tone stays audible and even.

Equalizer, Bass Boost and Hardware Upgrades

If the tone drops out early, use an equalizer to lift 40Hz to 100Hz gently, then retest after every change; a bass boost option helps, but over-boosting adds distortion. Still thin? Add a dedicated subwoofer to carry the lowest notes, since your audio system then gains headroom.

Safe Volume for Any Frequency Test

High SPL at extreme lows can damage audio equipment, so keep the sound modest. Streaming bass test songs for a car or gaming rig is fine for music and movies, but a bass test for speakers belongs in a pure free online frequency test like this one, where hearing and gear both stay safe.

faq.q: How do I test my subwoofer?

This browser-based speaker test sends audio tones through your speakers and headphones so you can set a comfortable volume level and catch a weak channel before music, calls or games begin. Every sound plays from your device.

What a Speaker Volume Test Checks

A speaker volume test plays signals at known steps so you can judge how loud, clean and even your audio equipment sounds. It confirms that your loudspeakers and amplifier respond when you raise or lower the level, and it lets you compare quiet and louder passages in stereo. A sagging channel or a fuzzy signal shows up fast. Use a left right audio test whenever one side seems weak.

How This Free Sound Test Online Works

This sound test online uses the Web Audio API to generate every signal inside your browser, so nothing is uploaded and your privacy stays intact. A sine tone, a frequency sweep and other test tones sound from your device on demand. White noise and pink noise act as reference signals: white noise adds a steady hiss across the spectrum, while pink noise is gentler to listen to. Playback starts only when you press a button, and each tone stops when you stop it. Pick a tone, raise the noise gradually and listen.

Speaker Test Options: Channels, Bass and Sweeps

Each check below targets one channel or one frequency band. Run the channels first, then move down to bass and across the range.

Left Right Sound Test for Channel Balance

Click Left, then Right, and confirm each sound comes from the matching side. The left and right buttons expose swapped channels, a silent right channel or a weak left channel. Equal loudness means good stereo balance, while an imbalanced result pulls the image to one side. If both stereo channels play but sound uneven, adjust the balance controls on your system and confirm the channel mapping matches your layout.

Bass Test and Subwoofer Response

Play the 60 Hz tone, then sweep the low frequency range from 20 Hz to 250 Hz. A subwoofer should keep going into sub-bass, while laptop speakers fade out early. If you hear no bass response below 80 Hz, your system has limited reach. Any resonance or rattling means something near the speaker is vibrating, so move it and repeat.

Frequency Sweep for Frequency Response

The log sweep glides from 20 Hz to 20 kHz and shows the frequency response of your speakers. Listen for a smooth rise through the midrange and treble; dips, spikes or distortion mark weak spots. Judge dynamic range by how clearly the quietest moment stays audible against the loudest. The spectrum spans about ten octaves, so a gap at any point is easy to hear.

Headphone Test and Earbuds

Wear your headphones and run the same sweep and channel checks. A good headset covers the full hearing range, while cheap earbuds lose deep bass. Tones should stay clear in both ears. Your hearing also changes with age, so treat this as a screening, not a hearing loss diagnosis; a clinical audiogram is the proper route.

Stereo Polarity and Audio Test Files

The audio test files here check polarity, which reflects how your speakers and amplifier are wired. When one speaker moves in while the other moves out, speaker polarity is wrong and bass cancels at the listening position. Reversed connecting wires cause it, so swap the wiring on one speaker only. Good polarity sharpens stereo imaging and sound localization. Room acoustics still shape what you hear from each seat.

In Phase and Out of Phase Check

Play the in phase and out of phase pairs from a central listening position. The correct pair sounds fuller, with more stereo separation, like a music recording playing in front of you; the other feels twisted inside your head and loses bass. If the out of phase pair sounds better, reverse one speaker's wires.

How to Interpret Your Audio Check Results

Read each result against what you hear. Both channels should sound clear and equal, and a sweep that drops off sharply at either end signals weak frequency response. A tone that wobbles or crackles can mean distortion. Rerun the same audio check after any change so the comparison stays fair, and note the frequency response you hear at each step.

Microphone Level Meter

The microphone meter shows live input with a peak hold. Speak normally and watch the level meter respond; no movement means a muted or disconnected microphone, and constant high readings suggest feedback. Keep peaks under clipping, around 70-90%. Use it to confirm each volume step actually reaches the microphone before a call.

Accuracy and Limitations of an Online Sound Test in Your Browser

Your speakers, headphones, system processing and ears all shape what you hear, and browser audio is not calibrated, so meters and levels here are relative, never exact readings. Use a calibrated sound meter for any acoustic or production decision. Treat this page as a first check of your audio system, equipment and hardware, and use proper calibration tools when precision matters.

From Left Right Audio Test to a 65 dB Night Level

I need my desk speakers quiet enough for 11 pm work without losing clarity, so the decision is a slider position. I start with the left and right check: both sides come up evenly, so the setup is sound. Then I play a steady tone at 100% and read my phone's meter from the chair: 82.6 dB.

That is 2.4 dB under the 85 dB occupational exposure guideline, so full volume is already the ceiling, not a safe default. My target for late-night work is 65 dB. The gap is 65 − 82.6 = −17.6 dB, and inverting the level formula gives an amplitude ratio of 10−17.6/20 = 0.132. So the slider belongs near 13%, which matches what the volume test showed me: low steps are far quieter than their percentages suggest.

I rerun the same calculation with nearby positions to see how touchy it is:

The number to watch is the move from 13% to 20%: seven points of slider add only 3.7 dB, so fine steps near the bottom matter most. I set 13%, replay the tone and read 65.2 dB, a 0.2 dB miss that I accept.

One caveat: the formula assumes the slider scales amplitude linearly, and many operating systems use a curved taper, so the percentage can land elsewhere. Phone microphones also read bass poorly, so I measure with a mid-range tone, not the 60 Hz one, and treat the result as a rough guide rather than precise data. If the reading disagrees with the formula by more than 3 dB, I trust the meter and adjust the slider until the target is met.

When to Run a Sound Test

Run a quick audio test before team meetings, after changing audio settings or when something just sounds off. It takes under a minute and shows whether the problem is your speakers, your device or the call.

Before Video Calls and Gaming

Confirm your speakers and headset are clear before important calls or a gaming session, because positional audio depends on clean stereo separation. Catching a dead side now beats hearing teammates say they cannot hear you.

Testing New Headphones

When you unbox new headphones or speakers, check the channels, the sweep and any subwoofer before your return window closes. A defect found early costs nothing; one found late costs the purchase.

Troubleshooting Results From an Audio Tester

If an audio tester shows one-sided audio, start with the simplest causes: cables, balance controls and your audio settings. Move the plug to another port, try another cable and rerun the test. Troubleshooting in that order separates a faulty wire from a software setting.

Bluetooth Headset and Audio Driver Fixes

If one side stays silent or the sweep distorts over Bluetooth, confirm the headset is the selected output, since a paired device can still route sound elsewhere. Then update the audio driver and allow the browser's microphone permission. Outdated software is a common cause of distortion and missing channels.

Safe Volume Levels During Speaker Testing

Warning: loud sounds can cause hearing damage after even one brief exposure. Start each speaker testing session at a reasonable level and raise it in small steps.

Keep Volume Below 85 dB to Protect Hearing

Long listening above about 85 decibels risks harm, and halving a signal's amplitude lowers the level by 6 decibels, not by half. Use this formula to see what each slider step does:

Sound Tester Glossary: Key Audio Terms

A sound tester relies on a few terms worth knowing.

Frequency response
The span of pitches a speaker reproduces, from deep bass up to 20 kHz.
Stereo balance
The relative loudness of the left and right channels; equal means centred sound.
Bass frequency
Low frequency pitches below about 250 Hz that need a subwoofer or large cone.
White noise
Equal power at every frequency, heard as a hiss.
Pink noise
Equal energy per octave, closer to how music is balanced.

faq_heading: Frequently Asked Questions About the Speaker Test Online

faq.q: Is the online speaker test safe for my speakers?
faq.a: Yes, as long as you start at a moderate volume and avoid sustained maximum-volume playback. The test tones are standard sine waves and noise signals — the same types used in professional audio calibration. Start at 25–50% volume and only increase if needed. If you hear distortion at any level, stop immediately and reduce volume.

faq.q: Why does the speaker test sound different at different volume levels?
faq.a: All speakers have a non-linear frequency response that changes with volume. At low volumes, bass frequencies sound thinner (the equal-loudness contour effect — the ear is less sensitive to bass at low levels). At high volumes, the speaker's physical limits cause harmonic distortion. This is normal speaker behaviour, not a fault.

faq.q: Can I use this as a subwoofer test?
faq.a: For subwoofer testing, the bass test is better suited — it covers 20–200 Hz with a dedicated sweep. The 1 kHz tone and frequency sweep in this speaker test focus on the mid-range. That said, playing white noise through all speakers simultaneously (including the subwoofer) gives a useful overall balance check.

faq.q: Why does the speaker test only play through one channel?
faq.a: Check your OS balance control first — it may be set fully left or right. Also verify your cable: a mono-to-stereo adaptor or a partially-inserted 3.5 mm jack will only output to one channel. If using Bluetooth, check that the speaker is connected in stereo mode, not mono/hands-free profile.

faq.q: Does the speaker test work with Bluetooth speakers?
faq.a: Yes. Select your Bluetooth speaker as the audio output device in your OS sound settings before running the test. Note that Bluetooth audio introduces 50–200 ms of latency — the tone will play with a slight delay after you click Play. This is normal and does not affect the volume or quality test results.

faq.q: What is white noise and why is it used in speaker testing?
faq.a: White noise is a random signal that contains all audible frequencies simultaneously at equal power. It's used in speaker testing because it exercises the full frequency range of the driver in a single pass. If a speaker has a weak tweeter, the white noise will sound muffled. If the woofer is damaged, the noise will have a hollow, thin quality.

Headphone Test Online: How to Run It in Your Browser

Because it works as a headphone test in browser, nothing installs and no sound leaves your device. Treat it as a quick diagnostic for headphones: it catches faults long before a warranty runs out and protects your hearing from harsh, mislabeled headphones.

  1. Plug in or pair your headphones, preferably over a wired connection.
  2. Start quietly: set the system and tool volume low, then raise it slowly.
  3. Play each test tone and move the pan control, the panorama slider, from left to right.
  4. Note anything odd and read the matching section below.

Any reliable headphone tool can reveal wear that you cannot hear in everyday listening, because familiar songs hide small sound faults.

Left-Right Test: Are Your Earbuds Wired Correctly?

Begin with the left right audio test, also called a left right sound test: play the left channel, then the right channel, and each should sound only in its own ear. A left right test headphones pass means your headphones are wired correctly. If it fails, check these results:

  • The channels are swapped or the earcups sit the wrong way round: sound arrives in the opposite ear.
  • Both sides play together: the signal is mono, often from a 3-pole plug in a 4-pole socket or a cheap adapter.
  • One side is quieter: open your sound settings and center the balance slider before blaming the headphones; check the wiring next.

Run an earphone test or a headphones test the same way for any model, since the channels logic never changes.

Stereo Test and Channels Check

The stereo test plays both channels of your headphones together, so a centered tone confirms matched output and good stereo balance.

Frequency Test: Your Headphones From Bass to Treble

The frequency test uses a sine sweep or a frequency generator to cover the hearing range, roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz, also written 20,000Hz. In hertz, bass extension shows how low the drivers reach and treble extension how high; a good frequency range in headphones covers both without gaps, as frequency is the core of every musical notes scale.

BandRangeWhat to listen for
Sub-bass20-60 HzA felt rumble, not a rattle
Bass60-250 HzWarm, tight thump
Mid (speech range)250 Hz-4 kHzClear, natural voices
Treble4-20 kHzCrisp detail without hiss

If the highest tones vanish, suspect your hearing loss from age first, and an odd skipping sweep may point to aliasing in your sound card.

Bass Test: Sweep the Full Range

A slow sweep in a bass test shows dips or peaks; the shape of the frequency response matters more than any single note.

Spectral Flatness and Earbud Insert Test for Earphones

Spectral flatness means no frequency sounds louder than another. The earbud insert test matters most for any in-ear design, because insertion depth reshapes the frequency response; a headphones (and earphones) test at a very low level reveals the depth that sounds flattest.

Driver Quality Test: Driver Matching on Your Headphones

Driver quality depends on tolerances. Driver matching means both drivers respond equally, so a sweep stays centered; a wandering tone points to mismatched units. The bass shaker sweep exposes any rattle or rattling part, and buzz or buzzing is the other common sign. A square wave and short bursts uncover resonances, distortion and harmonic distortion; reduce the level when the test tone turns rough.

Polarity Test

A low tone should push both drivers outward together; weak bass suggests reversed polarity.

Phase Test

An in-phase tone sounds centered, while out-of-phase sound feels thin and diffuse.

A Left Right Audio Test on a Pair of Used Earbuds

The decision: keep a second-hand pair of earbuds bought for $38.40, or return them within the seller's 14-day window. I plug them into my laptop with the cable, set the tool volume to 35% and open the left right audio test first.

Left plays a clear tone. Right plays it too, but a reading of the tone against my ear says it is quieter. That gap is the whole story, so I put a number on it by ear-matching the right side against a reference tone until they sound level: the right earbud needs about 3.5 dB less attenuation. Using amplitude ratio = 10(-3.5/20), the quieter side is playing at 0.668 of the louder side's amplitude. Roughly 1 dB is the point where most listeners begin to notice a level difference, so 3.5 dB is clearly audible, not imagined.

Then the sweep: the tone stays steady until it fades out at 15.8 kHz. Against the 20 kHz ceiling most spec sheets quote, that is log2(20/15.8) = 0.34 octave missing, a minor treble shortfall that many adults share with perfectly healthy earbuds, so I do not count it against them.

CheckResultVerdict
Left vs right level3.5 dB gap (0.668 ratio)Fault or source issue
Treble limit15.8 kHz (0.34 octave short)Acceptable
Swap test (earbuds reversed)Quiet side stays on the same earbudEarbud fault

The sensitivity rerun decides it: I swap the earbuds between ears and repeat. The quiet sound moves with the earbud, so the laptop's balance is innocent and the right driver is the problem. That is my judgement call: the number to watch is the gap, not the treble limit. One caveat: a gap that stays on one side instead points to the source, so a swap test always comes before any return. Next action: message the seller today with the 3.5 dB result and request the refund before day 14.

Soundstage Test and Stereo Imaging on a Gaming Headset

Gaming depends on the soundstage your gaming headset creates, and headphones differ widely: good stereo imaging places a tone outside your head, and soundstage imaging on a grid proves it. The binaural test adds depth, which helps with 3D audio and spatial audio. Over-ear headphones usually win for gaming and studio use; on-ear headphones trade space for portability, and soft ear cups and fresh ear pads help the seal.

Dynamic Range and Isolation in Closed Headphones

The dynamic range step of this headphone tool measures isolation: play noise, then a quiet voiceover that steps down in dBFS. The lowest level you still catch shows how well your headphones shut out the room. If the quiet steps vanish early, either your closed or open design leaks sound or the room is loud, and loud decibels from speakers nearby will skew the result.

Audio Latency and Microphone Test for Wireless Headphones

Audio latency is the delay between action and sound. Wireless links over Bluetooth add latency, and dropouts mid-test mean interference. For podcast or recording work, run the microphone check as well.

Headphones Not Working? Troubleshooting Fixes

When headphones not working is the problem, start troubleshooting with a firmly seated cable in the jack and a clean plug; earwax on tips quiets one side. Static or crackling when you move the cable means the wire is failing, and your headset may need repair. Use the speaker test to rule out the output device.

Judge Your Headphones' Sound Quality With Music

After the tones, play familiar music. Good sound quality shows in clear vocals, clarity without mud, a bass thump that stays tight and smoothness across the sweep. Listening to a concert recording through a proper amplifier shows how the audio quality holds up, and good polarity keeps the stage intact. Test your headphones every few months.

Press start, check the sound, and follow the prompts. The 3-minute hearing test plays a series of tones, and you respond each time you hear one. The on-screen prompts then show what you heard, with recommendations and next steps.

Headphones or Device Speakers

Choose headphones when you can. Unlike device speakers, they test your right and left ears separately, which gives more accurate results. Set the volume to the highest level that stays comfortable, and if you wear hearing aids, remove them before you begin.

Preparing for a Hearing Test Online

Take the test in the comfort of your home, with the TV off and no conversations nearby, so nothing competes with the softest tones.

Find a Quiet Place

A quiet place matters most: background noise hides faint tones and makes your hearing look worse than it is. Close windows, silence phone alerts and sit still while the tones play.

Hearing Test Results by Hearing Loss Level

The World Health Organization grades hearing loss by the softest sound you hear, measured in decibels (dB). Under 20 dB is normal, 20-34 dB is mild hearing loss, 35-49 dB is moderate, 50-64 dB is moderately severe, 65-79 dB is severe, and 80 dB or more is profound. Moderate or worse in the better ear counts as disabling hearing loss.

Take an example listener who hears tones at 20, 25, 20, 30 and 35 dB in the right ear, averaging 26 dB (mild), and at 35, 40, 45, 50 and 55 dB in the left, averaging 45 dB (moderate). The gap between ears is the finding to raise, because only a professional can confirm the type and severity or give a diagnosis.

Grading Your Father's Online Hearing Test Result

My father keeps turning the television up, so the decision I am making is simple: does he book an appointment now or retest first? I sit him in the spare room with headphones, run the online hearing test, and write down the softest tone he catches at five pitches. Right ear: 20, 20, 25, 45 and 60 dB. Left ear: 25, 30, 35, 55 and 70 dB.

The five-tone averages are 170 ÷ 5 = 34 dB (right) and 215 ÷ 5 = 43 dB (left). On the World Health Organization bands that makes the right ear mild (20-34 dB) and the left ear moderate (35-49 dB). Because the better ear is the right one, he does not meet the WHO disabling hearing loss definition, but he is a single decibel from it.

That one decibel is why I rerun the arithmetic before trusting the grade:

ScenarioRight earLeft ear
All five tones34 dB43 dB
Drop the 8 kHz tone27.5 dB36.25 dB
Noise adds 5 dB to every tone39 dB48 dB

The row to watch is the last one. A noisy room, or a loose headphone cup, would push his right ear into the moderate band without his hearing changing at all. In my judgement, the steep high-pitch drop-off matters more than the grade: his 8 kHz readings are 60 and 70 dB, so the averages overstate how he copes with low-pitched speech and understate how much he misses consonants.

The next action is specific: retest tomorrow in a closed room, and if the left ear still averages 35 dB or more, book a hearing care professional, because an online screen cannot say why the two sides differ.

Signs of Hearing Loss a Hearing Screener Can Flag Early

Catching changes early makes them easier to treat. Common signs of hearing loss include:

  • Difficulty hearing other people, especially on the phone
  • Asking people to repeat themselves
  • Turning up the volume on the radio or television
  • Listening fatigue after a day of concentrating

Left alone, mild hearing loss can raise dementia risk and leave you feeling isolated. Anxiety and strain on mental health and well-being often follow.

Online Hearing Test Limits Versus an In-Person Test

This check is not a substitute for a professional hearing test, and it is not a medical diagnosis. Only an in-person test can establish the cause of what you hear.

When to See a Hearing Care Professional

Book a hearing care professional if the result flags a concern or you notice the signs above. They can fit hearing aids if needed and guide your next steps.

faq.q: Can this replace a professional hearing exam?
faq.a: No. This is a screening tool, not a clinical audiological examination. A professional audiogram uses calibrated equipment in a sound-treated booth and measures your hearing threshold in decibels at each frequency — information this browser test cannot provide. If the results concern you, or if you notice a significant left/right difference, see a licensed audiologist for a full evaluation.

faq.q: Why do I need headphones?
faq.a: Headphones allow the test to play each frequency to one ear at a time and block out background noise that would otherwise mask the softest test tones. Laptop speakers and phone speakers mix both channels together and pick up room echo, making left/right comparison impossible and low-frequency results unreliable.

faq.q: What does it mean if I can't hear high frequencies?
faq.a: Not hearing frequencies above 14,000–16,000 Hz is common in adults over 30 and is usually normal age-related decline. If you cannot hear above 10,000 Hz, or if you notice a significant difference between your left and right ear, consult an audiologist. Loss of speech-range frequencies (500 Hz–4 kHz) is more clinically significant and warrants prompt evaluation.

faq.q: What is an audiogram?
faq.a: An audiogram is a chart produced by a clinical hearing test showing the softest sound (in decibels, dBHL) you can detect at each tested frequency. It maps your hearing thresholds across the speech-critical range (250 Hz–8,000 Hz). This online hearing test produces a simplified version — a frequency range display — rather than a full audiogram with dB measurements.

faq.q: How accurate is an online hearing test?
faq.a: Online hearing tests are approximate screening tools. Accuracy depends heavily on your headphones, your room noise level, and volume calibration. Studies suggest consumer-grade online tests can estimate hearing thresholds within roughly 10–15 dB of clinical measurements under good conditions. They are best used to track changes over time and to flag potential problems — not to diagnose hearing loss.

faq.q: Why are very low frequencies (below 40 Hz) hard to hear on this test?
faq.a: Most headphones and earbuds cannot reproduce frequencies below 40–50 Hz accurately due to the physical size of their drivers. Even if your hearing is perfect at those frequencies, your headphones may not be able to generate the sound. If you want to test bass-range response, use a full-size over-ear headphone or a dedicated subwoofer test with the bass test tool.

faq.q: What should I do if my results show a left/right difference?
faq.a: A consistent difference between ears — where one ear clearly hears higher frequencies than the other — is called asymmetric hearing loss and warrants professional evaluation. It can indicate wax buildup on one side, a middle ear problem, or (rarely) more serious conditions. Use our audio latency test to rule out equipment-side issues before concluding the difference is in your hearing.
